speechtext:
Mr. Speaker it was very refreshing to have the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), just back from the front, where he did such valiant service, tell the house and the country something about the thoughts and aspirations of the men at the front. May I congratulate and commend him for the contribution he has made and the courage he has shown in not being afraid to point out the defects in the rehabilitation plans at present operating, and express the hope that the government will take early remedial action in regard thereto.
Intimately connected with this subject is the question of housing. I am going to refer to that for a moment because it was mentioned in the speech from the throne.
Of the various acts respecting this subject, one was passed in 1935 called the Dominion Housing Act; in 1937 there was another act, called the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, and in 1938, the National Housing Act. I will deal only with the latter.
I would like to quote first from sessional paper 122T, laid on the table on July 6 last. On page 9 it is stated that:
Part II of the National Housing Act was designed to assist local housing authorities, including limited dividend corporations, to provide decent, safe and sanitary housing to be rented to families of low income which could not afford the "economic rental" for such accommodation. Under section 18, subsection 2, a provision was included that no loans might be made and no contracts entered into after March 31, 1940.
It is claimed that certain objectives, however, were achieved; in particular, progress was made in promoting a better understanding and appreciation of the nature and purpose of low rental housing and in working out some of the problems and details involved in this type of undertaking. I am sorry that the act was allowed to lapse in 1940, because I think it might very well have been continued until the present. I am well aware, of course, that the argument will be adduced that the war was on and we had other things to attend to.
May I for a moment recapitulate the events in connection with this low-cost housing programme. The present government, by order in council on May 13, 1936 appointed the national employment commission with Mr. Arthur B. Purvis as its chairman. Amongst other duties it was asked to "formulate regulations regarding practical measures for increasing employment." I cannot pass without paying a word of tribute to Mr. Arthur
The Address-Mr. Bruce

B. Purvis for the tremendous energy he displayed during the two years he was engaged in this work, giving freely of his great ability and business acumen to a labour of love. Although all his recommendations have not been implemented, his work will stand as a great contribution to our national life. From the interim report of the commission of which he was chairman, I quote as follows, under "Housing Construction," page 11:
The commission recognized the desirability of a rounding out of governmental housing policy, particularly as regards accommodation for those unable themselves to afford an economic rent -often associated with slum clearance. Action in this field was considered necessary both from the viewpoint of eliminating a social sore all too prevalent, especially in the larger cities, and because of its effect in stimulating employment in the construction field.
The commission recommended that the dominion and to a certain extent the provincial contributions should be in the form of direct subsidies, or, alternately, loans at a rate below the commercial rate, leaving to the municipalities contributions largely in the form of direct monetary payments equivalent to but not in the form of tax exemptions.
On September 9, 1936, the dominion government based certain principles upon recommendations made by the national employment commission. These will be found on page 101 of the commission's report issued on January 26, 1938. It was then announced that the principles which should govern that section of this broad housing plan to be devised to meet the requirements of those unable to pay an economic rent often associated with slum clearance, should be as follows: (a) participation by the dominion, by provinces or municipalities in any aid that may be given, whether by subsidy, loan, guarantee, or omission of taxes; (b) encouragement of the participation of private capital.
Then the commission, on February 9, 1937, presented its detailed plan to the minister, feeling that dominion government action was justified at the time for the following reasons: ' (i) As a measure of public health and social advancement, low rental housing projects will have a direct influence in imporving conditions of life for the low wage earner in urban areas and will be a factor in increasing the employability of our workers after a period in -which their employability has been greatly reduced;
(ii)	The field of low rental housing is the only one in which a direct and decisive stimulus can be given to home building without the risk of subsidizing competition to private builders and thus discouraging more building than is stimulated;
(iii)	The employment created by such housing projects will be greater and more widely spread than that afforded by large scale public works.

I have referred to the fact that to encourage building corporations to undertake this form of building under this part II of the National Housing Act, the dominion government was being asked to lend money to limited dividend companies at a lower rate than that prevailing in ordinary commercial loans. Such corporations might very well decide to limit their dividends to a smaller amount, especially if they received such long-term loans at a low interest rate. .
To give in a few words the need for slum clearance in low rental houses, I cannot do better than quote from the report which was madte in 1934 by a committee of which I was chairman. In that report we said:
Bad houses are not only a menace: they are active agents of destruction. The committee is satisfied, from its investigations and inquiries, that they destroy happiness, health and life. They destroy morality and family ties. They destroy the basis of society itself by their destruction of self-respect and their promotion of delinquency and crime.
Until slum clearance and rehousing of slum tenants is undertaken as a national duty and responsibility, to be discharged by national policies put into effect on a national basis, we shall quite unnecessarily be condemned to pass through all those very costly experiences which other nations have already passed through before being confronted by the ultimate inescapable truth that without government assistance there can be no effective slum clearance and rehousing of the lowest wage earners.
I find towards the end of the report that we urged on the dominion government that no public grants are so urgently needed as those for the rehousing of the poorest members of the community, and1 that, in order to make such grants -most effective, a national housing commission should be appointed to assist the-provincial and municipal housing authorities in the formulation of -plans, in the choice of materials, and possibly, if a nation-wide housing scheme can be initiated:, in securing economies by the large-scale purchase of such materials.
I hope the government will revive this portion of the National Housing Act by amendment or otherwise; for I believe the time has arrived when municipalities and limited-dividend housing corporations will be anxious to provide this form of housing by taking advantage of the opportunity to secure dominion loans at less than commercial rates for a period of thirty or forty years.

The Address-Mr. Bruce
I wish now to turn for a few minutes to another subject which was dealt with yesterday very effectively by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White), the subject of the rehabilitation of returned men. The national council of veterans' associations of Canada, after making a thorough investigation of the subject, made certain recommendations to the government. Let me refer for a moment to these.
Formerly the clothing allowance of soldiers on discharge wras as low as $17 if granted in the summer, but afterwards it was increased to 135. The council of the veterans' associations recommended that an allowance of $100 , be given to men with, overseas service; secondly that $75 be given to men with more than six months' service in Canada; thirdly that a wardrobe reconditioning allowance of $35 be given those with less than six months' service in Canada; and that the personnel of women's services should be given equal allowances.
The recommendations of the national veterans' councils are a minimum and do not provide for working clothing. Immediately following the presentation of these recommendations the clothing allowance was increased to $65, but I still think that this is inadequate and that the sum of $100, as recommended by the veterans' associations, should be the minimum, because it is quite obvious that $65 would not. do more than purchase a suit of clothes and an overcoat.
The present regulations provide for a grant on discharge of one month's pay and allowances. The national council of the veterans' associations in Canada has recommended to the government that rehabilitation grants of one month's pay and allowances be given for each six months of completed service. This seems to be more equitable. It is fair to assume that the longer the service the more time will be required for readjustment into civilian life. The present scale of dependents' allowances does not permit the accumulation of any surplus by dependents of men on active service, nor has it been generous enough to more than take care of essential living expenses.
Under these circumstances it will be found that on discharge or demobilization money will be required to reestablish families on a prewar basis. Length of service will have a direct relationship to reestablishment cost.
Now a word in regard to the hospital allowances during treatment. Formerly service personnel were discharged during the period of active treatment when they became wards of the Department of Pensions and National Health, with consequent serious impairment
of their financial situation. Now the regulations in part correct this injustice, but they do not go far enough. The national council of veterans' associations in Canada has recommended to the government that in no case should pay and allowances of a former member of the forces in this war, in hospital, be less than those of his rank during active service for the whole of his period of initial continuous treatment. This will ensure equal treatment for all ranks if adopted, and it would seem to be just without being overgenerous. It is advocated that no officer or man be discharged from the services until he is discharged from hospital; in other words that he should be given the moral stimulus of considering himself on the strength as long as he is suffering in hospital from war-time disability.
The present regulations are unfair for the following reasons: First, they discriminate against officers of higher rank than a lieutenant; secondly, they limit the benefit of full pay and allowances to a period of one year, or the length of service of the recipient, whichever is the lesser; third, they do not take into account the cases of men who may be discharged from hospital prematurely and have to return later for further treatment. A point should be made of the necessity of establishing proper regulations with respect to all matters of rehabilitation now, when there is general public sympathy with men on active service. When the war is over they will again be faced with public apathy, and I am afraid indifference, so that it will prove difficult to have regulations revised to correct any half-way measures which may be adopted at the present time.
I should like to say a word in regard to the promise made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) in respect of the Sunnybrook hospital which is to replace Christie street hospital. I understand that progress is being made in the preparation of plans. Early construction of this hospital however will depend upon the energy shown by the minister and his department. If the plans have to be completed to the last detail before tenders are called there will be a long delay in actual construction. May I say to the minister it will be possible to start construction within a month or six weeks if the government is anxious to do so and will allow tenders to be let on a fixed fee basis for profit, established on a reasonable estimate of the ultimate cost. The government should assume responsibility for any fluctuations of price of material or increase in wages of labour during

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
(he period of construction. Priorities for all types of material and equipment should be secured immediately and orders, placed as soon as quantities of specific requirements are determined.
Increasing numbers of seriously wounded men resulting from the operations in Italy and elsewhere will soon be coming back to Canada. Present accommodation is quite inadequate, so that Sunnybrook hospital will be absolutely essential at an early day. May I therefore urge upon the Minister of Pensions and National Health that he do his utmost to expedite the construction of this building at the earliest possible moment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had hoped on reviewing the speech from the throne to find in it some concrete proposals, but I am inclined to be of the opinion of a great many other members in this house that the speech contains just a lot of propaganda material which can be used to great advantage in an election. The more I read it, the more carefully I examine it, the more I am forced to that conclusion. One thing, however, which is outlined in the speech from the throne, and it appears in the first part of the speech, is I think, very commendable. It is that we are to continue to have an all-out war effort; or probably I should more correctly say it is hoped we shall have an all-out war effort. I do not think anyone can honestly say that we have had an all-out war effort up to date; certainly not from the time the war started, because I can well remember speaking in this house of an all-out war effort when the war started. We of the Social Credit New Democracy party were the only ones in this house who took a stand for an all-out war effort. We are still proud of that record, and we are grateful that we have made at least a dent in some of the thick skulls which opposed us at that time when we were talking about an all-out war effort.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: An all-worn-out effort.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is an all-worn-out effort; but I am speaking of an all-out war effort. I think that one of the grandest factors which must be considered in ar. all-out war effort is public morale. I listened with a great deal of interest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he spoke at the beginning of this session in regard to the war effort. He condemned those who went about the country preaching that the war was almost over. I think that was the proper stand for the Prime Minister to take. I am not one of those who believe that
	. . [
this war is nearly won. I recall reading the other day in one of our Canadian papers an article reprinted from a United States publication, to the effect that one of the United States generals had said that the German army was stronger to-day in man-power and equipment of all types than it ever was. I think it would be better for us to take that mental attitude than the attitude which might lead us to believe that the war is about over and we should relax our efforts. You can scarcely pick up a newspaper in Canada, even since the Prime Minister spoke, without seeing that some official has said the war is likely to be over this year. I remember reading a statement issued by General Montgomery just a day or two ago to his troops in England saying that he hoped and expected that this war would be over this year. That is in direct opposition to what the Prime Minister is trying to establish. We should begin to censor some of the statements that are made at home, in order to encourage an all-out war effort.
One of the other matters mentioned in the speech from the throne in regard to an all-out war effort is the total use of our resources. I do not think we have begun to use all of our resources in that regard. I recall oil, for instance. In my opinion we have not begun to develop the oil resources that could have been developed in western Canada, and which would have been of great asistance to us in our allout war effort. Another important point in regard to an all-out war effort is to see to it that public morale is kept up to the maximum and that we are using every available man in this country to the best advantage. The department which can perform that function to the greatest extent is the department which has control of the selective service boards. In my opinion the selective service boards are in some instances a disgrace to this country. I do not particularly blame the minister in charge, but I do blame the officials who are administering these boards. I had occasion to visit one of the selective service boards of this country-and I will name it, the one in Calgary-in an endeavour to get a farm boy, who could be spared from the farm for the winter months, a place in an essential war industry. As I entered that selective service office I was not very well impressed with the set-up. It seemed to me that the officials behind the counter were endeavouring to frighten the men who came in to make application. That seemed to be the atmosphere of the whole place.
I want to give the history of this case in order to show how this works out. This boy was given an indefinite postponement for work

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
in agriculture; and after he had been partly hailed out last year and had taken off the remainder of his crop, he made arrangements with his father, who lives not far away, to take care of his stock in order that he might accept employment in other essential industry. The government was continually asking farmers to do that very thing. This boy came to see me, and I said I thought that was a very commendable step to take. He had been offered a position in the Kimberley mines of British Columbia, he told me, at a salary of $175 a month, and he asked what he should do. I said, "The first thing you must do is go in and consult the selective service board, who will make the proper arrangements for you." He went in to consult this board and came home and told me the result. Then I went in personally to interview the officials of that board, and I must say that the attitude of those officials was anything but conducive to getting boys on the farms to take employment in essential industries. One official told me that he had informed this young man that he should go to the lumber camps if he wanted to work. The boy told him he did not have any experience in lumber camps and did not want to go there, that he had been offered this other job already. Then this official told me, "These boys must remember that they are in the army, and if they do not go where we tell them to go we will push them back into the army." Such threats should not be permitted. I pointed out that this boy was not in the army in any sense of the word, and that no official of the selective service board had authority to put him into the army. This boy came to me again to see what he should do, and I replied that I did not know. His answer was, "Well, if he thinks I am going up there to work in the woods when I already have a job offered to me, he is wrong." I said I did not blame him, and then he said, "I will go home and sit down, then; I will not do anything." I said I did not think we had quite reached that point, and I sent a wire to the deputy minister, Mr. MacNamara, asking if this was the policy of the government, and stating that I did not think it was. I received a wire in reply saying that they would investigate the case and let me know. That was over three months ago, and I have heard nothing since. I got in touch with one of the district agriculturists of my province, and we talked this matter over. As a result this boy went to British Columbia, regardless of our selective service board; he went to the mine and had his position confirmed, then went to the selective service board, who immediately put him on the job, and he started to work. Why should people be required to get out of 100-17
the province altogether in order to assist our war effort? I am not particularly blaming the minister, but he must take the responsibility because he is in charge of the department.

speechtext: Frankly I think that young fellow should be in the army.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Because I do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This young man has two hundred acres in crop; he has fifty or sixty head of cattle and forty or fifty hogs. Now the minister says he should be taken out of that essential industry and put into the army, though the government and the minister have said time and again that if these boys can possibly get away from the farm for a few months they should get out and assist in essential industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, but they have to go on the basis of priority; they cannot just go where they like. If that young fellow was in the army he would have to do what he was told; and if he wants to go into some other industry it is not asking too much to let us decide on the priority of that industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, here was a boy who was willing to do that. He went to the selective service board and they threatened to put him into the army if he did not go where he was told. Yet he had a job offered to him at good pay. Well, it is just as I said to the selective service official; this set-up is not a selective service, it is a gestapo. From what the minister tells me now I am more than ever convinced that this is so, and I can tell the Minister of Labour that there are thousands of young fellows who are anxious to get off the farm during the winter months and assist in essential war industries, and who would do so but for the bureaucratic dictatorship administered by the selective service board. If you want an allout war effort you will have to change your attitude. I have run across some funny things this last year, especially in connection with selective service, but the minister thinks it is fine.

You just go ahead and stick up for it; you are the only one who does so, as far as I know. I do not mean that the whole selective service organization is carried on like the branch at Calgary, but I do suggest that the Calgary office needs a little housecleaning.

When I was down at Drumheller I was speaking to the manager of one of the mines there who asked, "What kind of outfit is this selective service board"? I tried to outline what I thought of some of them-

Somebody says it is the "neglected service," and I think that is a better description. The manager of this mine told me that last year, when they were short of miners, they applied to Ottawa to have some miners sent out, and as a result five men were sent from the east, with their fare paid all the way. Three of them were >
old men, and after working three shifts they were declared physically unfit to do further mine work. Then they were given transportation all the way back to Ottawa. Why could not these men have been properly categorized and given a proper physical examination before sending them three thousand miles across Canada, when our railway trains are supposed to be so overcrowded? At least that would have obviated the necessity of bringing them all the way back east at government expense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: At the taxpayers' expense, you mean.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, the government are supposed to represent the people.
If we are to have an all-out war effort I think there will have to be some changes in the attitude of the government toward some of the returned men, veterans not only of this war but of the last war and their depen- t dents. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) went more fully into this question than I intend to go, but I would like' to draw one particular case to the attention of hon. members of this house. I know that some men who are fighting overseas to . save democracy have dependents in this country who are barely eking out an existence.
I had one particular instance brought to my attention, and concerning which I have communicated with the department. But it is only typical of others I have received. According to the regulations, if a boy happens to be overseas, or in the forces at some other point, and his father or mother are dependent upon him, the mother cannot receive any dependent's allowance unless the father is totally incapacitated from earning a living. When one realizes that the dependents' allowance board has to function under those regulations, he realizes that it is placed in a bad spot, no

matter how desirous it may be of correcting an evil. These old people may be receiving a very small allowance, possibly only $5 a month. The father may be working as janitor in a school, and as such he may be earning $5, $10 or even up to as much as S50 or S60 a month. In any case it is an amount insufficient to provide them with a decent standard of living. Under the regulations, however, the mother is prevented from receiving any dependent's allowance unless her husband is totally incapacitated from earning a living This means he must be an absolute pauper. If he is earning as little as $5 a month they cannot receive the allowance. Surely that is a condition the department should consider and change.
Provision is made in the speech from the throne for the setting up as a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada, of an industrial development bank to provide credit facilities for both fixed and working capital, so that industries may be converted from war-time to peace-time operations. I believe the government is to be commended upon endeavouring to take some action to facilitate the transfer of industry from a war-time to a peace-time *basis. My experience in the war expenditures committee gave me some insight into the tremendous productive capacity of Canada. All the factories we visited had the very best of equipment, and were doing good work. I shall not say anything about the quality of work being turned out, or the extent of production, but the point I make is that we have facilities right at hand, now to put out after the war a production unequalled in our history. It can be done, if we make the proper use of our facilities.
We note that the industrial development bank is to be set up as a subsidiary to the Bank of Canada. This morning I happened to see the Ottawa Citizen of Tuesday, February 8, and I noted particularly a misleading statement. This is what I read: "Bank of Canada cuts rediscount rate; debt-free money and ending fight for markets urged by Lord Sempill." I showed this heading to three men and asked them what it meant. Their reply was, "Oh, the Bank of Canada is cutting the rediscount rate, and they are going to issue debt-free money." Ninety per cent of the people are headline readers and I believe many persons across Canada after reading that headline are going to say, "Well, we are beginning to have some sense. The Bank of Canada is issuing debt-free money." But when one looks through the article he finds that it states something entirely different, and that no great change is intended at all. It states that the rate of discount will be* lowered from 2J to li per cent, on advances to

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
chartered or savings banks. This is no great reform. Once the chartered banks get the advance from the Bank of Canada, they can expand their credit from ten to twenty times, and the rate works out to only a fraction of one per cent. It does not in any sense indicate that either the chartered banks or the industrial development banks will be in a position to make loans to industries or agriculture at a lower rate. Unless we have some means of issuing national money for a national eause we are going to fall into the same error as that into which we have fallen many times before. The government seems to take a great deal of pleasure in passing the buck to industry, if I may use that expression.
There is a widespread belief that the onus of taking up the slack in respect of unemployment should fall upon industry. Industry cannot and never will absorb all the unemployed in Canada. We had better understand that right now, because such is not the function of indiustry, nor was it ever intended to be. As I pointed out a while ago, the industries of Canada are well organized, and they are turning out the necessary production. The war has proven their ability to produce goods. I am not saying anything about the profits they are making, nor am I expressing any opinion as to whether they are making too much or too little. That is a matter entirely for control. The function of industry is to produce goodis, and it is doing that. But to expect industry to give back jobs to all the men who have gone overseas, and who before enlistment were employed with those industries, is just pure nonsense. They cannot and they will not do it.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) delivered a good speech the other day, in which he encouraged the development of industries in western Canada. With his views in that respect we from the west entirely agree. He pointed out the potentialities accruing from such a programme. But one must always have in mind the markets to be supplied. There is no use in having industries, and a greater production of goods, unless we have markets in which to sell those goods. Why, even in the years of depression there was no scarcity of goods in the stores. Industry was producing as much as it could sell.
I recall visiting a plant in Canada just before the war, and upon returning to the manager's office I said to him, "Why do you not keep those fellows employed for the full twelve months of the year? Surely your mental make-up is not such, that you would deliberately dismiss a man and place him on relief for six months in the year, with the possibility that he and his family might starve." "Well," 100-174
he said, "no industrialist would take that attitude ; he would be inhuman' if he did." He showed me the great pile of stores in their warehouses, and said to me, "If you will get these goods out of here, I will put the men back to work very quickly-and for twelve months of the year." He was perfectly right.
It is the government's obligation to see that we have markets for these goods. Once we have the markets we shall have no difficulty in securing their production by industry. The assumption that foreign markets are going to solve our problems is, to my mind, quite wrong. True, foreign markets are necessary to a certain extent. We must have them so that we may exchange our surpluses, the goods which cannot possibly be consumed within our own country. The greatest and probably the most important of all our markets is the one at home. But in order to have a home market sufficient to take care of our population, we must have the purchasing power in the hands of the people so that they may buy back the consumer goods produced for them by industry. Unless we do that, we shall find difficulty ahead.
That purchasing power can be made up in several ways. A large portion of it can be supplied through industry, which pays the wages and salaries, but there is never enough paid out by industry in wages and salaries to begin to buy back the products of industry, and so there is always a lag. We have advocated the issue of national dividends to make up that lag. Every other party in the house has criticized and ridiculed this principle of national dividends. In view of that, it is amazing now to see in the speech from the throne mention made of family allowances. I have not heard anybody criticize them. Family allowances are in part a national dividend, but only to a very selected portion of our citizens. I am waiting with a great deal of interest to hear what the rank and file of the Liberals supporting the party which proposed these family allowances have to say about that. The principle of the family allowance is sound. But when you issue a family allowance to only a portion of our citizens, that is discrimination.

speechtext:
My first word to-day will be to the
men and1 women of our armed! forces; of the navy, the army, and the air force; those who are serving us in all parts of the world, fighting to preserve our freedom; and not overlooking, too, the doctors and the nurses who are rendering such wonderful service. Our casualty lists are heavy, and we fear will continue so. Our

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
thoughts go out in deepest sympathy to those at home who have been bereaved of loved' ones. They are examples of the great fortitude which must be the strength of the nation in these serious times. Our sailors have endured the rigours of the ocean in all kinds of weather and under extreme difficulties, never knowing when they might face the submarine or the enemy from the air. We cannot but pay the highest tribute to those heroic men who night after night go out and fight our battles over Germany. Our tribute goes too to the men of the army in these trying days, in the difficult situation, they face ini Italy.
These men and women, who have been training now over several years, are acquiring an entirely new outlook on life. Men from the maritimes have visited as never before our Pacific coast. Men of the Pacific coast have visited, in training, our eastern provinces. Many of them also have found that their training has taken them to distant parts in the neighbouring republic of the United States.
The course of training during this war has been entirely different from that in the previous war. This is a war of science and mechanization. Consequently our men, when they return from this war, will come back with a knowledge of mechanics and, in many respects, of science which they never had before. We must remember that; we must keep pace with them, realizing that their point of view will not be that of the men and women who left us to go into training and into battle. When they come back to Canada they will find different conditions also. They will find a prosperous country. Men and women have been working for good pay and under good conditions. They have had money to spend and have enjoyed a measure of prosperity despite the difficulties of the time. Our war effort has been huge. There may be things we can criticize, but the word that comes from other countries, from great leaders elsewhere, is always that of praise for the magnificent effort that Canada has put forth in this war. The men will find when they return that conditions are not as they were after the last war. They will find that prices have been controlled1 and that the country will not be facing a period of reduction in prices and1 losses of inventories, as was experienced in 1919.
Prosperity makes prosperity, and in the prosperity that has been created in this war we . can see the great value of creating, in the world that is to be, conditions under which our men and women will have continuous employment. We will welcome them back to better conditions, and it will be our problem and responsibility to see that those better conditions are maintained.

Many of the men will come back to join their brides of the early days of the war, or perhaps to bring brides with them from the old land. There is a great responsibility for us in the way of assistance in setting up new homes; for, as has been said here so frequently, the home is the foundation of the nation.
I say therefore that in all our arrangements for the future, and for these men and women as they return, we must take into account the fact that they have a changed point of view, and that they will be determined that in future there shall be no repetition of the disappointments that followed the last war. We owe a great deal to these men. Our men were at Dunkirk, at the fall of France, and they took part in the battle to save the British isles, which no doubt prevented the enemy from reaching our shores.
What I have said, Mr. Speaker, with regard to consideration for these men as they return, and the efforts to rehabilitate them, goes also for our most generous consideration, as the days go by, for the veterans of 1914-18 who even yet may be experiencing difficult conditions. I am not one who is learned in the law but I have had considerable business experience, and so it has been natural, during the eight years or so that I have been in this parliament, that I should think along the lines of business and business procedure. That trend of thought has led me as an observer to be irritated at times perhaps with the methods of parliament and the business approach to the consideration of the expenditure of money, and so on. And so, with this attitude, I was prompted, back I believe in 1937, to introduce into this house a resolution calling for a revision of the rules of the house. I mention this to-day7 because already a committee has been set up to consider means whereby the procedure of parliament may be improved.
It has always seemed strange to me, and I suppose it is the way in politics, that all of one party should vote one way and all of another party should vote another way. That apparently is necessary under our system of government, whereby the defeat of any measure means the defeat of the government. We may not agree with some particular measure, but according to practice it seems that if we oppose that measure in sufficient numbers the government which we support on the sum-total of its efforts may be defeated.
My attitude has been to take an independent view of the questions that come before us, and that will always be my attitude. I feel that I am here to represent all my constituents and not only those who voted for me. It has been my desire therefore to see an improvement in the rules governing procedure in this house

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
which will leave me freedom to vote for the measures I approve and to oppose the measures I cannot approve. In order to make my attitude clearer on many of the questions that are before us to-day I have had it in mind, following the practice of political parties, to set down a number of points that represent my way of thinking on the questions of the day.
My theme in general is this, that with an improvement in procedure, so that members of parliament may consider legislation on its merits, and with provision to make corrections where there may be weaknesses in our methods and weaknesses in legislation, we can draw upon the past to build for a better future.
I do not see the necessity of uprootingvthe past in order to have a prosperous Canada in the future. I think we can rely on the past, with adjustments and corrections, so that there will be opportunity for every man and every woman to make a decent living in this Canada of great resources. Therefore I desire to enumerate briefly a number of points to indicate my way of thinking and the course I would wish to pursue as the member for the riding of Wellington South.
1.	Christianity is our accepted conformity to the divine purpose. Encouragement, in government, to things Christian, and discouragement of things unchristian, is the sure foundation of national worth.
2.	National individuality develops with the lapse of centuries. To-day Canada is a growing force in the British commonwealth of nations. In that sphere we can exert a powerful influence, in association with the United States of America, for peace and good will amongst all peoples.
3.	Unity of purpose of our peoples of many origins can be attained best by a policy that will encourage a blending of the races in an atmosphere of understanding of civil and religious freedom.
4.	Parliament should aim to promote these ideals in our development as a nation. There is need for recovering the confidence of Canadians in their parliament as an institution for safeguarding and promoting equality of rights and equality of opportunity for all.
5.	To this end members of parliament, especially in this time of world crisis, ought to exercise their right to advocate and consider legislation with less regard to party affiliation. Members now have freedom, in theory but not in general practice, of voting according to their judgment. Consequently I advocate that the defeat of a government measure shall not constitute defeat of the government.

6.	Confidence or want of confidence in the government, after non-acceptance of proposed legislation, should be determined by a separate vote. An adverse majority on a confidence vote would then constitute defeat of the government.
7.	Speeches frequently are ill-prepared, irrelevant and wasteful of time. Reduction in the time allotted for speeches, with certain exceptions, should be made.
8.	Procedure in parliament should be revised to minimize general debate. Procedure in committee should be revised to broaden members' opportunity of scrutinizing departmental administration and to give parliament a greater measure of advance control over expenditures. Calling departmental officials before committees would stimulate efficiency and sometimes, perhaps, unearth situations unknown to the ministry.	_
9.	The civil service system should be revised for better recognition of merit and vice versa as to incompetence. There should be flexibility whereby persons with essential qualifications can be sought for special work.
10.	Senate reform is being called for in many quarters. Members of that body might very well take the initiative in organizing, in a non-partisan way, for an enlarged programme of national service during the entire session. Unless the public is assured of greater usefulness the demand will grow for change to an elected senate.
11.	Agriculture is becoming more and more a scientific and mechanized vocation. Our colleges must be financed more generously for the best obtainable facilities and equipment and to attract specialist personnel for skilled service and leadership. Prices to the farmer must be scaled upwards. His profits will flow back into purchases of machinery, better houses and barns, electrification and modern conveniences. These needs will contribute to employment in industry.
12.	Forest reserves in Canada are being depleted by fire, insects and destructive logging methods. Steps must be taken to institute scientific methods and sound business policy to maintain and increase our forests.
13.	Mineral production in Canada has expanded enormously for war purposes due to the diligence and skill of the prospector and the scientist. Canada's northland is a vast prospect largely untouched. We must , give all possible encouragement and support to those who seek out and develop its hidden treasures. Active mining production means increased factory operations.
The Address-Mr. Gladstone

14.	Merchant shipping is a war-created industry of Canada capable of much expansion. Our trained seamen will respond to this new opportunity of sailing Canada's products to the ports of the world and back with much needed cargo. Qur fisheries resources, both salt water and fresh water, are unsurpassed anywhere. Our rivers await harnessing to turn the wheels of industiy.
15.	Air transport is another war-created industry of Canada. We are the link between the world areas of most dense population. Just as our brave airmen have conquered in war, so will they serve in jjeace for all mannei of transport via our Atlantic to Pacific resources of the air.
16.	The tourist trade in our playgrounds of the north is a potential resource of Canada capable of enormous expansion. I suggest that thousands of the temporary war-time houses be reerected along our lakes and rivers in colonies as tourist homes. Under direction we can have these as attractive summer homes for visiting Americans and as comfortable stopping places for our own citizens on vacation. Colonies of tourist homes could be made to give all-year employment to an ex-service man as supervisor, storekeeper, postmaster, et cetera.
17.	Boys and girls, especially in our cities and larger towns, should be given the advantage of physical training for health, deportment, and discipline. For confirmation of the value of such training, see members of any branch of the armed forces. They have a glow in their cheeks. Their shoulders are squared. They walk with evidence of purpose. They know the importance of team work.
_ 18. Our prisons are becoming comfortable -lading places for those who would escape miliary service. These and many delinquent youths should be set to work under guard in lumber camps and mines. Besides board and lodging they should receive modest wages, the same to accrue for assistance to dependents or for themselves by instalments on release to assist them to a new start along better lines.
19.	Warning is given that the public is becoming critical of overstaffing of army and other officers in Canada; likewise at headquarters overseas.
20.	Warning is given that many men who have been in the reserve army for two or three years consider it futile now to spend time at a summer training camp.
21.	Warning is given that after the war our continuing organization for reasonable defence precautions should not be permitted to grow into a costly military aristocracy.

22.	Canada occupies a strong position for industrial development of the aforementioned resources through abundant power, an advantageous world location and a virile people. Persons or corporations must not be permitted to gain monopolistic control. The remedy lies within the power of parliament. Maximum industrial progress can be assured best by encouragement to vision and to the pioneering spirit of our people in association with modem science in a system of due recognition of individual initiative and enterprise.
23.	Finance is a service for exchange of values and should be made to serve that purpose at fair cost to all. Persons or corporations associated with finance must not be permitted, through interlocking directorates and in other ways, to adopt policies detrimental to the maintenance of employment on a balanced keel as opposed to cycles of prosperity and depression. Again the remedy lies within the powers of parliament. Canada should aim to be financially independent of other countries.
24.	Labour, both men and women, merits the praise of the nation for its contribution to the war effort. Canada will be richer with better paid working men supporting, more comfortable homes, better clothed and better fed children and an assurance of security if sickness comes or when they can work no longer. I shall support every fair means possible that our workers may have assurance of the four freedoms.
25.	Government proposals for security are on a huge and unprecedented scale. Before the present war the total annual expenditures of the federal government for all purposes, including pensions and veterans' allowances, was around 8550,000,000. The estimated cost to-day of the far-reaching programme of social security and veterans' rehabilitation as outlined in the speech from the throne approaches $600,000,000. This amount includes, according to forecasts, $300,000,000 for veterans' gratuities, allowances, rehabilitation, et cetera; $150,000,000 for family allowances and $75,000,000 for national health insurance. Additional amounts in various fields will be provided by the provinces. This surely is an answer for those who are wondering if money can be found for needs in peace time as it has been found for war.
26.	There is need for establishing better the supremacy of parliament. Why the methods of careful business administration cannot be employed in parliament is more than I can understand. This criticism is directed towards all governments, past and

The Address-Mr. Burton
present, federal and provincial. Perhaps it is that regimentation of members best serves political ends. I call for commitee scrutiny that will reach into places and situations probably unknown to ministers.
27.	It must be apparent .that I support democracy freed of hidden selfish direction, either from individuals or groups. I take the past, make corrections and build for the future. I stand for fair and equal opportunity for all men to exercise their initiative and their qualities twice beneficially, to themselves and to the nation.

speechtext:
Mr Speaker, on this, my first opportunity of speaking in this house, I wish to express my appreciation to you and all other hoa. members on both sides for the very kind welcome that has been extended to me as a new member.
At the very beginning let me frankly state that one of the main reasons I am here is that last year in Saskatchewan a group of men took it upon themselves to deny to the citizens of that province the democratic right of passing judgment upon the stewardship of their elected representatives, by extending their own term of office without the consent of those whom they govern. Why did not this government exercise its powers of disallowance, when the democratic rights of the citizens of the province of Saskatchewan were interfered with, as promptly as it did when the special privileges of certain financial institution? in the province of Alberta were threatened? Speaking on behalf of the people of the constituency of Humboldt-yes, and on behalf of the majority of the people of Saskatchewan-through you, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the government to disallow that act extending the life of the Saskatchewan legislature, which is one of the darkest blots on the annals of any democratic country. It is the very negation of democracy. Even though it is somewhat late for such action, I contend that the disallowance of this legislation is the least that can be done to remove that blot and to avoid the establishment of a dangerous precedent that might make a farce of our democratic system of government. On Monday, January 31, I was pleased to hear the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) state that he did not approve the idea of parliament extending its own life. I now appeal to him and to his ministers to take the necessary action to restore to the people of Saskatchewan their democratic rights. Some may argue that this government should not interfere in the domestic affairs of any province. In reply I say that the democratic rights of any part of this
dominion should be of greater concern to us than the special privileges enjoyed by financial institutions.
There are other reasons why the electors of Humboldt constituency decided that they could no longer support this government. In the past they were prepared to march down the aisle to the altar of political union with the Liberal party to the strains of "Oh Promise Me", but that day is gone The people of Saskatchewan realize that the Liberal record has been a series of broken promises. While any fair-minded person realizes that in these trying times it is most difficult for any group of men to conduct the affairs of government, yet such fairness ceases to be a virtue if the people would continue to tolerate the inefficiency of this administration. When political expediency takes precedence over the safety of our country; when political patronage supersedes justice, then the people demand a change.
The great majority of the people of Humboldt constituency are farmers, and even most of the residents of the towns and villages depend for their livelihood on the purchasing power of the farmers. The greater part of this territory was settled some forty years ago by people of many races and creeds working together in a neighbourly way to carve out of the wilderness homes for themselves and their children. Scarcely had the sod shacks and log houses been constructed in a community before the neighbourhood got together and built a place of divine worship. They had faith in God; they loved their neighbours, and their desire was to have the opportunity to establish homes and raise their families in peace and seourity. With visions of comfort and security in the years to come, these pioneers cleared and broke large fields and raised enormous crops. Situated on the edge of the park belt, part prairie and part bush land, and dotted with many small lakes, the greater part of this territory never had a complete crop failure. Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of new wealth were produced in grain and live stock. These provident, hard-working people did not squander their money. Their homes are very modest; in fact many are quite inadequate to their needs. Very few made trips to California, and fewer still back to the land of their birth. But after all these years of hard toil, do you find these people enjoying the well-earned comfort and security that they are entitled to? Many are still struggling along, doing work far too heavy for their advancing years. Others have been forced to give up the struggle and eke out a drab existence under the so-called old

The Address-Mr. Burton

age pension, while the great majority of them have only a load of debt to pass on to their children.
When an industrious people cooperate with a bountiful Providence with no better results than these, then there is something wrong somewhere. This may give hon. members some idea of what I mean. From the book "Down North" written by the British High Commissioner for Canada, Right Hon. Malcolm MacDonald, I quote:
Such people have made Canada. They love the open spaces and their passion is to produce the fruits of the soil. But they sow the seeds also of greater things. Other people come after them and gather that harvest.
Though the right hon. gentleman wrote those lines in describing one small group of people with whom he had come in contact, they are equally descriptive of practically every farming community in western Canada.
Ever since the west has been, settled the policies of the two old political parties have made it impossible for the farmer in the west to obtain a just return from the fruits of his labour. In spite of glowing promises, Liberals and Conservatives allowed their friends from other parts-yes, from other lands-to reap the harvest. These pioneers and their descendants still have faith in God. To produce the fruits of the earth is still their passion, but they have lost confidence in this administration.
For the information of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I can assure him that his Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), with all the resources and help at his command, left no stone unturned in trying to convince the electors of Humboldt constituency that the agricultural policy foisted on the west by this government w^s in their best interests. But for once the Minister of Agriculture found himself without a band wagon; so that finally in desperation he climbed on to the water wagon. For years the citizens of the town of Humboldt have been in need of an adequate water supply. Water for domestic use is being hauled to the town by tank wagons. For a number of years both the Canadian National Railways and the town council have made extensive but unsuccessful searches for the source of an adequate water supply. Just two days prior to the by-election last August, supporters of the Liberal party, carrying in honey tins samples of water which were alleged to have come in from some test holes several miles out of town, canvassed the town. Their stock-in-trade argument was that they were prepared to admit that the C.C.F. was going to win the constituency, but that the Minister of Agriculture had promised that if only the town of Humboldt would give the

Liberal party a majority the necessary funds and the priority for pipes would be made available. The town of Humboldt did give my Liberal opponent a majority, although it is quite true that their former majority of 400 or 500 was cut down to around 30 votes. Nevertheless, the fact remains that the town did give the Liberal party a majority. What I wish to know is this: When is the Minister of Agriculture going to fulfil that promise?
While the citizens of the town of Humboldt were being given the water treatment by the Liberal board of strategy, the Minister of Agriculture's henchmen covered the constituency, promising each community according to its local desires. For example, in some sections they tried to lead the people to believe that an all-out war effort could be entrusted only to a Liberal administration and its supporters, while in other places the argument used was that the Liberal candidate was the one who could get their boys out of the army. However the electors refused to be sidetracked from the real issues, and voted want of confidence in the government, on the following grounds:
1.	The failure of the government to protect the democratic rights of our citizens;
2.	The hampering of our war effort by allowing the profit motive to dominate the war industries;
3.	The refusal of the government to place agriculture on an equitable basis with other essential industries;
4.	Failure to solve the man-power problem, and
5.	The hampering of our farmers and small business men by unnecessary and bureaucratic restrictions and control.
On this occasion it is not my intention to deal with all these matters, because other hon. members have already dealt with some of them. But, as a farmer, and as the representative of an agricultural constituency, 1 wish to speak on behalf of the farmers. For a great number of years the farmers, with justification, asked for better grain prices. This was denied them, for one excuse or another. In later years we have been told that we could not have those higher prices because it would break the price ceiling. What the farmers would like to know is why their prices were frozen at less than the cost of production. .On the other hand, spokesmen for the Liberal party urged the people that if they wanted a better deal for the west they should send more Liberal members to parliament.
I have been rather busy in the few days I have been in Ottawa, and have not had

The Address-Mr. Burton
time to count the Liberal members from the prairie provinces. However there seems to be quite a number of them, and I have come to the conclusion that my colleague the 'hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) and myself have more influence with the ministers than all these back-bench Liberals put together. The ninth of August had a startling effect upon the administration. It suddenly became aware of the fact that the farmers in the west meant business. Practically over night, ninety-cent wheat became dollar-and-a-quarter wheat. Roughly estimating this year's crop at a little less than 300,000,000 bushels, the farmers are about $100,000,000 better off in this one year alone because the electors of Humboldt and Selkirk refused to be kidded any longer.
There is no reason why that increase in price could not have been made five years ago. During that time the farmers producing grain have been penalized to the extent of at least $500,000,000-and, Mr. Speaker, out in my part of the country that is a lot of money. It would have helped to pay off quite a few mortgages. However I wish to warn the Minister of Agriculture that he and his government have not yet redeemed themselves in the eyes of western farmers. The maximum production of bacon has been seriously jeopardized by the hesitating and inadequate action of the government. The bonus for top-grade bacon hogs recently announced by the minister is just another example of too little and too late. We have heard quite a bit about hogs during the course of this debate. It is not my intention to elaborate on that. On the one hand, my colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) showed that the producers of hogs were just about being rail-graded out of business supplying the export market. On the other hand, I should like to know about the pork products consumed in this country. Why is the producer of heavy hogs being penalized to the extent that he is? At least, why do not the consumers get the benefit? Do the consumers have the opportunity to buy any of this pork cheaper because it comes from heavy hogs?
Another matter of vital interest to western farmers with which I wish to deal is the unfair allotment of railroad cars for shipping grain. We all realized the urgent necessity during past years of making full use of all available storage space, and we were prepared to cooperate to fill up that space even to the extent of hauling some of our grain to elevators with which we did not want to do business. But having filled that space once, we object most strenuously to being compelled to refill that space time after time and to being denied1 the 100-184
opportunity of delivering our grain to our own elevators. For example, at some points in the west, before this quota and car allotment system came into effect, our elevator handled from seventy-five to eighty per cent of the business, where now, through this unfair car allotment system, our volume has been forced down to forty per cent, and in some cases as low as thirty-five per cent. Someone somewhere, with the blessing of this government, has been playing sugar-daddy at our expense to the very interests that are opposed to our cooperatively owned elevators.
The other day I was pleased to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) announce that we were to have more cars allotted to where we needed them. Following that announcement I received a telegram from a man at Humboldt who had made it his business to find out just what the situation was in two municipalities in which there are ten shipping points, and he reports that of these ten shipping points seven are still without sufficient cars to enable them, to handle their quota. He sent me a covering letter giving all the details, and after I am through with it I shall be pleased to give the details to the minister.

I
shall be glad to have them.

speechtext:
Those two municipalities
constitute only a small part of my constituency, and Humboldt constituency is only a very small part of the west. When we have seven out of ten shipping points short of cars to handle the quota in only two municipalities, and we have fifty shipping points in Humboldt constituency, what about all the rest? I have not had an opportunity to make inquiries, but I am going to make it my business to do so, and I am going to take the minister at his word and inform him as to every shipping point that is short of cars.
Another thing that alarms me is that the agricultural policies of this government are forcing the family farm' out of our national economy. More and more are we being forced on to a mass production basis. The only way the farm family can compete with modern mass production is by the use of the unpaid slave labour of the women and children on the farms. If it were only that the family farm was in danger I would not be so much concerned, but the very existence of the farm family is being severely threatened. Remember, the family unit is the very foundation of our nation, and statistics prove that the farm family is the keystone of our national life.
The family allowance forecast in the speech from the throne, if properly put into effect,
26S
The Address-Mr. Burton

will be of some assistance, but in itself, it cannot preserve the farm family. In addition, with the rest of the people of this country, we are entitled to know if this and the other legislation forecast in the speech from the throne is just another dream by the dreamer of twenty-five years ago.
I should like to say something about the man-power problem, but to deal properly with the man-power muddle we are in would take much more time than I have on this occasion, and I shall have to leave most of my remarks on that subject for some future occasion. I want to say this now, that if the government in their wisdom consider it necessary for the safety of our country to have fewer men on the farms and more men in the army, then let them say so, and then the farmers will know what is expected of them. But the government cannot expect us farmers to continue to produce the amount of foodstuffs which we are asked to produce unless provision is made to retain at least our experienced help.
In addition to that there are many farm boys who have already, I believe, spent sufficient time in the training camps, and wdio could now be allowed to return home on extended leave, subject to immediate recall in case of emergency. They would be of greater service to their country helping their folks at home than they are at present, kicking their heels around in these camps, with no place to go.
We have stepped up our production to the very limit of our present farm population, and to do that, the farm families are being driven beyond their endurance. Already there are signs of decreased production. This statement is confirmed in a pamphlet "Canada at War", No. 32, of January, 1944, issued by the wartime information board, on page 51 of which a table is shown giving the agricultural output per male farm worker. The table takes 1939 at 100, as a base, and shows that in 1940 and 1941 we had only eighty-nine per cent of our male workers left on the farms; in 1942 and 1943 we were down to seventy-five per cent. On the production side, again taking 1939 at 100, the table shows than in 1940 we produced 105 per cent; in 1941, 112 per cent, and in 1942, 186 per cent. That is a wonderful achievement. But at what a cost! I venture to say that the last three years have taken more than an extra ten years off the life of the average man and woman on the farm.
Now we come to the 1943 estimated production. With only seventy-five per cent of our workers left on the farms, we still produced

160 per cent of the 1939 basis. But we had an alarming drop of twenty-six per cent in our production from that of the previous year. Speaking in the Saskatchewan provincial legislature a year ago, I told the provincial minister of agriculture, who also acted on various boards for this government, that if they continued to drain our boys from the farms we could not meet the production goals set for us. A deaf ear was turned to my warning. But, Mr. Speaker, this table proves that I was right.
The question is, what are we going to do this year? In my opinion we are facing a still greater drop in production, especially in those lines most needed. I want to give just two examples of many which I could furnish right from my own constituency.
I have in mind one couple, a man and woman seventy years of age. They had no children of their own. They raised a nephew. When the war started that lad wanted to enlist. His uncle told him, "O.K.". The lad enlisted, but before he did so he made arrangements with a younger brother to take his place on his uncle's farm. The younger lad and the man proceeded to operate that farm. Right in the middle of harvest and threshing time that boy got his notice, his call, and he had to go-no ifs or buts about it. The old man told me, "Joe, if God continues to give me good health I shall be able to keep the weeds from running away with the farm, but I certainly cannot do the field work and at the same time do the necessary chores, with all this live stock, all these hogs that I have around. The result is," he said, "that they will have to go." That man carried on. I was seriously afraid that he would break down. Finally, this fall, he realized that he had to do what he said a year ago he would have to do; he had to dispose of his live stock. He used to have a considerable amount of live stock on his place, and now he has no more than he needs for himself and his wife. He is keeping the weeds from running away with the cultivated land; that is all, and more than all, he can do.
Another case: a man, who is now seventy-five years of age, for the past two years has stood on a tractor and operated the tractor and a 15-foot combine alone while his boy took the grain away from the combine. On that farm-again-they used to have live stock, hogs whose value ran into hundreds of dollars value every year. But these people could not carry on the other work which had to be done and at the same time do the necessary chores which live stock entails in our part of the country. What these people needed were, not

The Address-Mr. Jackman
high school boys and university students some of whom would not know a tractor from a combine, not that kind of help, but boys right from their own neighbourhood who would know how to operate and handle machinery, and which end of a cow to sit down to if they wanted a pail of milk.
