People of the Humboldt constituency have always been willing to do their part as citizens of this country. Enlistment records show that descendants of all racial groups in that constituency are serving in the various branches of the armed service while their elders are working and sacrificing to the limit of their ability to help bring about a victorious peace.
Within a short time we shall again be entering that season of the year when we commemorate the sufferings, death and resurrection of the Founder of Christianity. We also think of the sword of sorrow that pierced the heart of the Mother Mary as she stood at the foot of the cross and beheld her Son, the victim of man's wrongdoing, selfishness and greed. To-day for the second time within a quarter of a century the flower of our manhood, the youth of our nation, is being crucified on the cross of world selfishness and greed. What is yet in store for us no one can foretell, but this much is certain, the hardest part is yet to come. Before many months pass, many a mother will stand with her hands clasped to her breast, with a sorrow in her heart that only the mother Mary can understand. In view of this, the least we can do is so to fulfil our duties that these sacrifices and sufferings will not have been in vain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first present my compliments to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; and may I particularly compliment the hon. member from Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) whose few remarks in French seemed to my untrained ear to be more understandable French than that of those who learned that language at their mother's knee.
Not a word was said in the speech from the throne, however, about the restoration of the supremacy of parliament over the executive. When the War Measures Act became operative by proclamation at the outbreak of war, it was necessary that the executive be
given the power to legislate on the most vital matters affecting the life and security of our people. But after nearly five years, what a reflection on this government if it has not so organized the fighting forces and the production front at home that legislation by executive order should still be necessary! In the opinion of our people the executive is now an overholding tenant, tenacious and avaricious of dictatorial power. The exigency and need for haste in executive action without discussion among the people's representatives has long since passed. Surely the time has come when there should be some revision of the War Measures Act whereby the sovereignty of the people's representatives should be restored to them and exercised by them and not delegated to a handful of dictators who, in cabinet council, sit behind closed doors and order our people about as if they were no longer free men.
Typifying the methods of dictatorship of this government, which does not even consult its own mechanical Liberal majority, are the confessions of two Liberal members, one of whom said, in regard to order in council P.C. 9384 regulating wartime wages, "The government is run by a bureaucracy. The members are nothing, and I frankly admit it. If the order had gone through this house it would have been better prepared." And again, in answer to the remark that labour was being used as a guinea-pig for bureaucrats to experiment upon, a Liberal member said, "The members of parliament are dead guinea-pigs. I have never been consulted or called in on these measures. I admit there are powers behind the government and I know who they are." Assuming that the executive may still need emergency powers of dictatorship, does that excuse it for such flagrant abuses of such power? What an affront to the people's representatives! What a mockery of parliament! What a throwing of democracy into the discard!
The house leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) graphically pictured this bureaucracy by pointing out that since September 1, 1939, statutes passed by parliament have covered 838 pages, while proclamations, orders in council, war orders and regulations have required 5,791 pages-seven times as much legislation by executive order as by parliament. The people no longer run their own country. We are no longer a sovereign parliament. The government is a sovereign executive.
Mr. Speaker, very little has been said about that section of the speech from the throne which was undoubtedly inserted as a result of the speech by Lord Halifax. May I. however, correct an observation made by the hon. mem-
The Address-Mr. Jackman

ber for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) in moving the address. From his knowledge of Lord Halifax's speech-which from his deductions I doubt if he has read, but has on the other hand rather relied on press clippings and editorial comments from his local newspapers- he appears to labour under a misconception of the purpose and content of the speech. Wherein would he find justification for his statement that: "The latest edition of these mysterious travellers is attempting, it seems, to refloat the foundered ship of the imperial federation"; and, again, "to shower upon us instructions which we shall term indiscreet to say the least"?
The people of Canada as well as the people of the whole British empire, indeed the people of the whole world, are acutely concerned with the achieving of an enduring peace. If a distinguished representative from another country accepts our invitation to visit us, surely he is entitled to fulfil the purpose for W'hich he was asked to come, namely, to present worth-while thoughts for our consideration in respect of one of the gravest questions facing mankind.
As to the remarks of the member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), he seems not to have crept out of his colonial shell, which the rest of Canada has long since left behind. He said:
So far as I am personally concerned, I feel that we should continue on our course of moving toward complete sovereignty within the British commonwealth of nations.
Does the hon. member think Canada is anything less than a sovereign power and has been anything less for many years, with power to save its national life or to lose it? Rather let me agree withjhe speech made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) in Hamilton recently, in which he is reported as having said:
Canada is as much the master of her own foreign policy as is any sovereign state in the world of its same size; but neither Canada nor any state in the world can of course stand alone.
I think we shall admit that there are many >'mall states in the world which have full sovereignty; but there are few if any who, for i heir own protection, do not find it necessary to move within the orbit of some larger constellation, if not within the orbit of the whole universe itself. I hope no one in Canada will be so ignorant of our true constitutional position as not to know that Canada is a free and independent country. If membership in that great British commonwealth of nations was thought to be any bar to this view, I have only to point to the peculiar and invidious position of the free state of Eire, whose constitution is so closely modeled on our own. While the future lies ahead, our present autonomous position should be plain to all our fMr. Jackman.]
people. The decision taken at the forthcoming meeting of British commonwealth prime ministers will be far-reaching in its effect, affecting not only the destiny of the British empire but the destiny of the whole world. That decision may result in the strengthening of the forces for peace, or it may result in the beginning of the liquidation of the British empire, the greatest force for peace the world has ever known.
The people of Canada look forward with great1 interest to the amplification of the following statement in the speech from the throne:
You will accordingly be invited to approve of Canadian participation in the establishment of an international organization to further national security through international cooperation.
There is little on the international horizon, with the exception of the declaration of principle contained in the Moscow agreement, to indicate what that international organization is likely to be. The failure of the last effort, a failure due in part to the uncooperative and blind policy of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was adamant in his refusal to apply sanctions to Italy, just as was the United States at an earlier date to support coercive measures with force when Japan invaded Manchuria, leaves little to inspire one with confidence in a new but similar organization. Do we find our own Prime Minister at the present time taking the lead in building up any international organization such as President Masaryk of Czechoslovakia took after the last war? The end we all seek is plain-peace, prosperity and the right to live our own way of life. But I for one have no intention of grasping at the shadow and losing the substance. Our security and trade lie primarily within the British empire, and old friends are best friends. Our propinquity and close relationship to our cousins in the United States can be strengthened, as can the whole world position, through our membership, first, in the British empire, and secondly, in an international organization.
In that brilliant editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal this morning the theme was built around the following quotation: "No sight is more pathetic than to watch the perfect impede the good.", Are we to be placed in the position of refusing to give up some aspect of our sovereignty within the British family of nations for our mutual protection and then to be asked, to give up that same aspect of sovereignty to some international organization of strangers? If we cannot live as brothers within the British, family it is unlikely that we can live happily as an international club. Let us not bask in the idle undertakings of the President of the

The Address-Mr. Jackman
United States, who in his Ivy Lea speech before the war undertook to protect Canada from attack when he was unable to protect even his own country. Are we to rely on a big cousin who every time our common liberty is at stake finds himself shot through with the cancer of isolationism? The Royal Navy has always been the protector of the American Atlantic seaboard; and only the constant readiness of that navy-ready, aye, ready- and the unconquerable courage of the Royal Air Force in the battle of Britain have given civilization the chance to preserve itself while the North American continent armed itself for the conflict. Yes, and in those* pre lend-lease and pre-mutual aid days we and our United States cousins sent Britain a bill, to the extent of her ability to pay, for keeping the hun from the shores of North America. What a conception of international morality!
Turning to the domestic sphere we find that family allowances have been proposed in order to ensure a minimum of well-being and a closer approach to equality of opportunity to the children of this country. But one wonders why the government proposes this measure at the present time and if it is the intention of the government to implement that proposal immediately. It appears that in the mind of the government it is money that creates this closer approach- to equality and this minimum of well-being; but unless the treasury of this country is inexhaustible it may well be that there are more necessary reforms which should be given a priority over family allowances. In estimating the cost of those family allowances, Doctor Charlotte Whitton, one of the foremost sociologists in North America, placed the figure at $400,000,000. We do not find, however, in President Roosevelt's bill of rights any mention of family allowances. He gives other matters concerning social legislation first place. Doctor Whitton has made ten suggestions which should be given consideration before we embark on any scheme of family allowances costing $400,000,000 a year. Doctor Whitton recommends:
1.	More adequate protection for children without decent parental guardianship.
2.	Custodial care for feeble-minded children, especially girls and young women.
3.	Strengthening of family welfare and adult education services.
4.	Better housing for rural and urban homes.
5.	Electrical power and appliances for rural homes.
6.	Better nursing care in all homes.
7.	Enlargement of Canadian hospital resources.
8.	Improvement of elementary schools in other than urban centres. This, Mr. Speaker, is one of the crying needs of our great country.
9.	More free diagnostic clinics.
10.	Food subsidies.
Where is the $400,000,000 to pay for family allowances coming from? The people are going to pay for these allowances; for that is the only place where it can come from. The total share of the national income now going to investment income, to those who own government and other bonds, stocks and mortgages, et cetera, is less than ten per cent. If that ten per cent of the national income is where the horn, gentlemen of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation say it is, in great concentrations, then it is obvious to all that with a personal income tax rate which runs up to well over ninety per cent there is practically nothing left after the state gets its take. Since nearly every family holds a government bond or an insurance policy-there are over three million holders of victory bonds in this country-we know that investment income is very widely distributed and it is perhaps not unreasonable to assume that not more than half of it is taken by taxation. Thus, of the ten per cent of the national income going to pay interest or dividtends on the capital savings of the people, only half or five per cent would be left after the tax-gatherer has taken his as net income capable of being spent or reinvested. That does not leave very much for the government still to take. Even if capital were drained to the last drop it would not provide funds for more than a fraction of the social security programme outlined by this government.
If it is not obvious to all that the main burden will rest on the great mass of the people of Canada, then they should be told in no uncertain terms; for it is one thing to be delighted with gifts which other people pay for, but quite another thing to have gifts forced on one and then be sent a bill for the same at the end of the month, if the amount is not deducted from the weekly payroll. Is it any wonder, sir, that the president of the trades and labour congress, as well as the congress itself, inveighs against family allowances. Mr. Percy Bengough, president of the trades and labour congress, said:
The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada lias consistently opposed family allowance legislation. We are astounded that the suggestion is being made that workers' income be based on bare living standards to be increased by subsidies from the government according to the number of children.
They know who is going to pay for these allowances, and their fear is that the money
The Address-Mr. Jackman

will be collected at the source through some tax on industry, which, in the competitive struggle for world markets, will mean that their wage returns will not be as high as they otherwise would. Money, which is a claim on the goods and services of our fellowmen, does not grow on trees but is created by the sweat of the brain and the brow of the workers of this country, and the workers of this country not only are concerned with getting their fair share of the national income but in most cases prefer to spend that share as they best see fit, rather than to have a paternal government, no matter how well-intentioned, spend their own money for them.
At school one used to hear about the iron law of wages-an outworn' economic theory- whereby labour was believed never to receive more than sufficient to maintain itself and to reproduce its kind. Is this government suggesting that that is the best standard of life which it can promise our workers? Labour is entitled to a fair wage, and when I say "fair" I mean that labour is entitled to most of the benefits arising through new ideas and more efficient methods of production. It is sufficient to leave the owners and managers just enough to keep them saving and working their heads off and their hearts out improving the general standard of living. But never let us kill the goose that lays the golden egg; for it is leadership, whether in statecraft, industry or elsewhere, which gives life to the mass. Without leadership we are lost.' With fair wages and adequate unemployment insurance to cover any temporary period of unemployment, surely a worker can be paid enough to maintain himself and his family.
Family allowances undoubtedly have their uses, but unquestionably they have their abuses. Where the balance lies I am not prepared to judge at this moment; but if the people who are going to pay for it do not want this piece of paternalism I see no reason why it should be forced upon them.
The Prime Minister suggested that the speech from the throne divides itself naturally into three sections: first, the winning of the war; second, the transitional period from war to peace, and third, the resolutions for social security, presumably in the post-war period. It is important that we should know when the government plans to make operative a scheme such as family allowances, which at a time like the present is wholly inflationary in all its aspects. If one of the chief purposes of our victory loans is to drain off the surplus spending power which cannot be utilized because civilian goods are not available on which to spend it, then surely the pumping 
back of some hundreds of millions of dollars annually into the hands of the people at this time, through family allowances, will put a pressure on the price ceiling which will blow the lid to kingdom come. Is it any wonder that when the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), in seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne, mentioned that the government had found a way of effecting a much needed adjustment in farm income, through various measures for the financial benefit of our farmers, without increasing the danger of inflation, the colour in the face of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) mounted visibly? Perhaps the rosy effusion was for other seasons, but the coincidence was most marked, for no one knows better than the minister the danger of every hand-out to our people, no matter how well justified, is to the price ceiling. Greater than the wrongs which are sought to be remedied is the danger of inflation which may well be brought about by the very means used as a cure for the lesser evil.
When speaking on. the need for social security measures I have always expressed the hope that the Christian spirit of brotherhood among our people would be sufficient for them to be willing to introduce such measures as are necessary not only for the protection of those who are less strong but also for the protection of those who may be strong but who, because of the impingement of world events upon our economy, from time to time may suffer hardship. Some forms of social security measures undoubtedly are necessary because of our dependence upon world trade, as the fourth or fifth trading country in the world, and because we cannot be entirely masters of our own economy, whether that economy be capitalism, socialism, fascism or communism.
Let us look first at our whole social security programme. It must be based upon our postwar plans and outlook, just as the Beveridge plan for social security is based on not more than ten per cent unemployment. Instead of enacting social security measures piecemeal, let us sketch the whole canvas before filling in the detail and throwing the whole picture out of balance. Let the people of this country have a look at the total financial commitments they will have undertaken in regard to social security and other measures before they are asked to rush headlong along any one particular field. Health insurance I should consider an exception to this general rule, because the good health of the people not only reflects adherence to a humanitarian principle but is a sound investment.

The Address-Mr. Jackman
la the consideration of the over-all financial obligations we are about to undertake, let us have an eye to the means whereby they will be paid for. I have already declared that the great mass of our people are the only source left to bear the major part of the burden; but our people are also concerned with the rate of taxation, not only on themselves as individuals but on themselves as employees of business organizations which must be allowed to live if they are to give leadership in supplying the goods which will raise the standard of living and at the same time create jobs. If the government wishes to consider post-war planning it must consider first what kind of economy we are going to have. If enterprise is stifled through taxation burdens which kill incentive, then it is perhaps better that we should at once lose our freedom and become a totalitarian state rather than suffer a slow, lingering and blood-letting death through a policy which stifles all development and all new employment. In a recent speech Wendell Willkie said:
When peace comes taxes must he minimized rather than maximized in order to stimulate the flow of goods, the taking of risks and the creation of millions of jobs. We must solve the post-war tax problem, not by imposing the biggest possible rates on our income, but by creating the biggest possible income on which to impose relatively modest rates.
Let the government declare itself so that both small and large business men may know where they stand, so that they may plan for job creation. During the war there has been no need for new industries for the production of civilian requirements which would give our people a more abundant life. Indeed the demands of war production made it desirable that the dead hand of heavy taxation and priorities should be laid upon new business ventures for civilian consumption. With victory that position will change, and the business man must know where he stands if he is to create employment, a field in which he is particularly qualified to give leadership if he is not interfered with by political agencies whether they be of the national or international variety.
Time will not permit me to discuss socialism, but I point out that while this government makes no profession of state ownership of private industry, through its taxation measures not only has it captured one hundred per cent of all war profits of industry, which is perhaps as it should be, but it has cut itself in, through the minimum taxation on any business, to the extent of forty per cent of the average amount which that business earned in the four pre-war years 1936 to 1939. Thus the government takes not only all new profits, but forty per cent of all prewar profits even if the company is earning less than it did in peace time. And this, Mr. Speaker, goes one better than socialism; for the government bears no risk whatsoever of loss, and at the same time has never put up one cent of the capital which goes into the ownership and creation of those industries. Can business be expected to survive and develop under such conditions as those, under a "heads I win, tails you lose" policy, where there is no reward for the assumption of risk and there is thus no offsetting recovery for the losses which business sustains when the dreams and hard work of businessmen, whether in the field of industry or commerce or in the development of natural resources, go awry and the only dividends are losses?
The reference to the creation of an industrial development bank as a subsidiary to the Bank of Canada in order to provide both fixed and working capital for the conversion of industrial plants has not so far been mentioned in this debate, and I desire to make a few observations before the resolution is brought down or the bill debated. Indeed, while the government often borrows good ideas which are developed by the opposition in the debate on the resolution, it is even better to have suggestions accepted before the administration allows its preconceived notions to crystallize and thus obstruct the acceptance of a major change in principle or organization.
In the post-war period there will undoubtedly be many cases where an intermediate credit bank is both desirable and needed. The reconversion of war industry to peace industry -from production to kill to production to live-will entail many problems and many risks.
Despite the recommendation of the British Macmillan commission of 1931 and the need for such intermediate credit facilities in peace time, no great development ever took place. Being interested in the possibilities of such business in Canada, I called on the managing director of such a company in the city of London in 1937 and came away with the impression that while the idea was theoretically sound, it was practically of little value because of the great amount of time that had to be given to the oversight and operation of the small borrowing companies. In ordinary times it is not likely that the application of more than one borrower in twenty could be accepted. The post-war problem of Canadian industry may well be different and the bank's usefulness to the country in the transitional period 'from war production to peace' production need not be determined solely by the profit motive. speechtext:
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, before the conclusion of the debate on the address, I should like to make a few brief remarks on some features of the speech from the throne which, in my opinion, are particularly interesting.
I was glad to read that the government recognizes the family and the home as "the foundation of national life" and that "in order to aid in ensuring a minimum of wellbeing to' the children of the nation and to help gain for them a closer approach to equality of opportunity in the battle of life, the members of this house would be asked to approve a measure making provision for family allowances".
That matter was broached long ago and I do hope that the implementing of such a plan will not be indefinitely postponed. For some time, many rumours (which fortunately had no official character) were abroad to the effect that such allowances would be limited to a certain number of children in each family. I have every reason to believe that those rumours are groundless, and that the government will introduce into such a generous, humanitarian and necessary legislation no feature that might bring about a lowering of the birth-rate in this country.
I, for one, will heartily support that measure and I have no doubt that it will apply to all children. Does not that legislation aim at helping the heads of families, and especially those who have many children? At first sight, it is hard to understand any restriction in its application, because the heads of large families are generally those who are most frequently in need of government help.
In some European countries, and especially in England, the authorities having noticed, not so long ago, a steady lowering of the birth-rate and viewing with the greatest concern its direful consequences for the nation, have appointed a commission empowered to

The Address-Mr. Bourget
investigate the causes of such a situation and suggest possible remedies. I have no accurate recollection of the recommendations made by that investigating commission set up in England, but I am sure that a measure like the one providing for family allowances was suggested with a view to improving the situation and increasing the birth-rate. I do believe that were the principle of granting allowances-subject to no restriction, of course -adopted in Canada, we would soon notice the advantages of such a measure.
Another feature of the speech from the throne has particularly impressed me. I refer to "the measure to amend and supplement existing housing legislation".
With the hon. members who have already dealt with that matter-and I wish to single out my colleague and friend the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Durocher)-I wish to emphasize the serious problem that exists especially in centres where war industries are to be found. Such towns are now facing a serious housing problem which becomes more acute as the month of May draws nearer.
I know that many of our towns where dockyards are established have experienced a population increase. The housing problem has reached a point where it has become urgent that the government step in to help these municipalities whose financial resources render it impossible for them to solve this problem brought about by the war.
I have already, on many occasions, in the course of a year or so, discussed1 this deporable condition with some ministers, especially those from the vicinity of the city of Quebec. They are showing some interest in this matter and I hope my efforts will have practical results. Because of the urgency and importance of the conditions obtaining, I wish to call this matter lo the attention of the house.
It seems to me that the government should help these municipalities by granting subsidies that would allow persons who will be without a home next May to start building houses immediately. It may be said that the war will soon be over and that the towns will then have a number of unoccupied houses. I do not hold that view for, in my opinion, many of the people who have moved1 from rural districts during the last four or five years, to work in our cities, will stay in urban centres after the war and it will naturally be necessary to find hygienic and comfortable houses for them.
Another plan that might be considered by the government would be that of granting loans at a small interest, or 2 per cent, for example, in order to make it easier for those
of small means to get the funds necessary for the construction of dwelling houses. It might be advisable to set up an organization that would work and cooperate with the municipalities and individuals concerned.
In view of the urgent need of solving this problem, the government should see that such an organization is set up immediately to ensure that we shall not have to face a serious condition at some future date. Besides fulfilling an urgent need, such a measure would be very commendable from the social point of view, and, what is more, would help to increase the number of small property owners which unfortunately is at too low a figure. I hope the government will soon introduce a bill to remedy this evil or submit to the municipalities concerned some project in this connection.
Another matter on which I wish to dwell particularly, is the labour question, since I have the honour of representing in this house * a constituency, peopled mostly by workers, in fact, it is probably the best labour constituency.
Since the beginning of the war, we have unfortunately witnessed strikes and disputes of all kinds between employer and employee. I do not wish to be unfair to anybody, but, during the last few years, in the course of which I have been more closely associated with both employers and employees, I have been led to believe that the cause of all these misunderstandings do not originate exclusively from faulty legislative measures, but, above all from the lack of cooperation between industrial leaders and workers and mutual mistrust.
I am sorry to have noticed so often that some industrial leaders, trying at all cost to keep the workers in the virtual state of slavery-if I may so express myself-which existed before the war, do not seem ready to abandon this method -and will neither trust the leaders of trade unions nor cooperate with them for the purpose of improving their relations and thereby increasing production in their industries.
I should now like to point out that I do not claim the workers are always right, but I simply wish to mention what struck me during my interviews with company officials and workingmen, ever since I have had the honour of representing the constituency of Levis in this house.
It is quite logical to say that good legislation naturally helps to promote better relations between capital and labour, but I can state confidently that it remains ineffective until these two classes have developed good understanding and mutual trust.
The Address-Mr. Bourget

To my mind, the worker should be reasonable in his claims, and should work to the extent that his employers expect of him; on the other hand, the employers should show greater fairness in dealing with the workers and treat them not as hirelings but rather as collaborators and devoted servants.
I wish to state here that I am in favour of private enterprise. On the other hand, I warn those who are most vitally concerned in the maintenance of this system after the war to change some of the methods which they are using at the present time; otherwise, they will compel our leaders to exercise a more *rigid control over these industries so that better understanding may prevail in our industrial undertakings.
I take this opportunity to call the attention of the government, and especially of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) upon the administration of the various laws under his department. I have found that there was a lack of supervision in the administration of these laws. Commercial firms appear to have too much latitude, and they interpret in their own way, and frequently to their advantage, of course, the .various measures passed by the government.
Such methods naturally breed discontent within the labouring classes. Sometimes blatant injustices are committed and the government has no opportunity to intervene. I understand that the Industrial Relations Branch, which comes under the Department of Labour, is doing excellent work in this field. Unfortunately, it is inadequately staffed, and the adjustment of the grievances which are too frequently reported is unduly delayed. I have personally found that certain grievances have remained unsettled for two or three months due to the fact that this particular branch of the Department of Labour was short of inspectors.
I would therefore ask the Minister of Labour to see to it that his staff is increased so that any misunderstandings which may arise may be adjusted with as little delay as possible.
* In "Facts and Figures" published by the wartime information board, I read recently that:
On January 21, 1944, the honourable Minister )f Munitions and Supply and the honourable Minister of Labour released a joint statement announcing the recent establishment by order in council of an industrial cooperation board, entrusted with the duty of assisting and promoting the appointment of labour-employer joint committees in war industries.
Personally I am in favour of the setting-up of such a board. Production committees have already been organized in some industries.
TMr. Bourget.]
Representatives of both employers and employees sit on these committees. Unfortunately-and here again, due to the lack of confidence and good will between employers and employees-these organizations have proven ineffective. The employees, realizing that the suggestions which they were making in order to increase production and reduce costs, were not put into practice, simply discontinued, in some cases, to sit on such production committees.
Under the circumstances, the government's purpose in appointing such a commission is praiseworthy, but I hope that the new body will be able to function properly. Otherwise that new commission will not achieve results such as we might expect from. it.
I wanted to make those few remarks, Mr. Speaker, not for the mere purpose of criticizing private companies, but rather to help in the improvement of the relations between capital and labour.
I should like to say a few words on another matter; I know that we shall have an opportunity to discuss it when the budget is brought down, but, in passing, I request again the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to remove the tax on the salary paid for overtime.
I sincerely believe that the amount collected by the government in the form, of such a tax is not very large and that the removal of the tax would greatly enhance production. As a matter of fact, everyone realizes that such a tax has the effect of discouraging workers from doing any overtime.
Last year the Minister of Finance had promised that he would look into that matter. I hope that, when the next budget is brought down we shall have the pleasure of learning that such a tax will no longer hinder war production.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say a word about immigration? In my opinion that subject should be dismissed, at least for the time being, because its discussion proves useless.
We have noticed for some time past that some war plants were laying off thousands of employees on account of the lack of work. Therefore, nothing should be done that might increase the unrest and bring us back to the pre-war depression years. Before any immigration plan is considered, all our people who are physically fit should be given an opportunity to obtain work. Once the employment problem is solved, the immigration question can be considered, a wise selection being made as regards those accepted as new citizens of this country.
In that particular, we shall not be influenced by those pilgrims who come here

The Address-Mr. Knowles
every year to deliver speeches and teach us lessons. We are old enough to take care of ourselves, and I hope that authoritative advice along those lines will be imparted to such people.
Such, Mr. Speaker, are the few observations I wanted to make in this debate. Before resuming my seat, I should like to express the opinion that, when this war is over, the new world which will emerge will not be entirely free from poverty, hardship and anxiety. Nevertheless, with the help of the new beneficial legislation which is imperative and which will be administered with equal fairness to all classes of society, I hope we will be able to bring about and maintain a better understanding, which will be all to the good of the country. May this disastrous war soon come to an end, and may the good days of a beautiful and intense family life be restored to all homes which at present stand empty.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne has been hailed by the section of the press that supports the government as a remarkable document, full of promise for a better day. We of this group welcome its few good points, but we are in duty bound to point out its serious shortcomings. Our criticisms of the speech are in the main two. First of all we are skeptical lest the government fail to reduce the proposals contained in the speech to actual legislation to be enacted before this session ends. Our second criticism is one that, we feel is shared by the entire country, namely, that the suggestions in the speech do not begin to go far enough. They do not even scratch the surface of the tremendous problems facing us at the present time.
To turn for a moment to our first criticism, our scepticism as to "whether anything will be done following the giving of this speech, let me sail attention first of all to the kind of language in which the speech abounds. One paragraph starts something like this, that "in the opinion of my ministers," and so on, "plans .... should be advanced as rapidly as possible." Plans should be advanced! Further, certain things "are contemplated." We suggest, Mr. Speaker, that language of that kind, in the face of the tremendous problems which we had hoped would be dealt with in the speech from the throne, is adequate ground for our scepticism as to whether anything will come of this speech. Surely the phrase, that "a broad programme has already been developed for the k reestablishment of veterans," sounds hollow after the remarks of other members, particularly the speech yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). I find that another paragraph states that "the maintenance of full employment will require"-and a long list of things is given-but no suggestion is made as to how these requirements are to be met. There is another paragraph, to which attention has already been called from this corner, that states: "When suitable agreements are reached with the provinces, my ministers will be prepared to recommend" measures for social advancement.
Not only are we led to be sceptical by this language in the speech from the throne, but we take that position because of what has happened during the course of this debate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who usually speaks at considerable length in this debate and deals in detail with the items in the speech from the throne, surprised us this year by delivering a rather brief speech, by dealing hardly at all with the speech from the throne, and by failing completely to touch upon the paragraphs that suggest social security and other measures of post-war advancement. Not only has the Prime Minister failed to give us any dissertation concerning this glorious document, but not another member of the cabinet has risen in his place to outline for us the glories of the speech or to sell to us the proposals and the promises that are suggested in it.
We are told to-day that it is the desire of the government that the vote be taken on the address to-night. I assume it will be taken to-night or not later than to-morrow, and yet up to this point neither the Prime Minister nor any other member of the government has dealt with the suggestions in the speech from the throne which have excited the interest of the Liberal press throughout the country.
We are quite convinced that the speech, even if its suggestions were to be enacted, does not go far enough, and it is really a bitter disappointment to the people of Canada at this time. Canadians everywhere realize, whether the government does or not, that once victory has been won, there will be required on that day for Canadians almost two million jobs. We suggest therefore, whether that day is soon or even not so soon, that it is high time that some proposals were set forth to deal with that basic requirement of almost two, million jobs for Canadians when victory in the field has been won. It is on the background of that basic need that we feel that the speech is a bitter disappointment.
The times call for a really broad plan that will provide jobs, certainly not just for the sake of jobs, but that will also provide for meeting the post-war needs of our people, for seeing to it that our workers and farmers are given a chance to provide the things that are needed and also a chance to enjoy them when
The Address-Mr. Knowles

they are provided. We suggest that in the fields that are basic, housing, clothing and food, there should be enunciated at this stage plans that will provide for the employment of our people and in turn for the distribution of these things among our people for their enj oyment.
This war has taught us among other things the importance of the market here at home, and the needs and requirements of our own people. We have learned that particularly in the matter of food. We have discovered that whereas before the war we had huge surpluses, while some of us were pointing out that thousands of our people were underfed, now even with our productive resources in food being strained to the limit we are able to make use of all that we are producing1 because our people, in city and country alike, have better incomes and are able to translate their needs into an actual economic market for food. We suggest that, important as international trade is, valuable as it can be to the economic welfare of our country and to the countries with which we trade, the important thing is to see to it that we pay attention to the market to be found in the needs of our own people. It is on that basis that we are highly critical of the speech from the throne brought down in this critical year, at this critical stage of our history, with these tremendous problems facing us, with the experience of the war, in which we have learned what can be done by national organization, yet with no suggestion that the government is prepared to institute economic planning in such a way as to provide jobs for our people and the things that our people need.
_ I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, in connection with social security, to which there are references in the speech from the throne, but no promises of any measure except the measure relating to family allowances. This measure has been brought in along with a restrictive labour policy, P.C. 9384. This governments labour policies have made organized labour wonder whether this otherwise desirable social service is being brought in simply as a substitute for an adequate wage policy. Apart from that one measure, the other references to social security which are found in the speech from the throne are so many pious promises and suggestions as to what should be done, what is contemplated and so on. The fact is that social security can only be provided adequately if we have an economy that is functioning to its maximum capacity. I do not wonder that the ministers have not risen in their places to discuss the speech from the throne. There is nothing 
definite there to discuss along the line of social security and post-war social progress. When they do start to discuss these plans and suggestions for social security they will have to give us some hint or at least answer questions as to how such schemes are to be provided and maintained. The fact of the matter is, if we are prepared to establish economic planning and social ownership of the basic means of production so that we can put our economy on a full-fledged basis, then literally there is nothing in the field of social security that we cannot provide if we have a mind to. The question of how it is to be paid for largely disappears. We of this group have pointed out again and again that social security is not something that is to be had for nothing. It has to be paid for; but the real cost of social security, like anything else that a community has and enjoys, is to be found in the labour that people expend and in the raw materials we use. We have these things in this country, vast labour power, tremendous resources of raw materials. IVe are asking in the name of the better world for which this war is being fought that there now be given us a plan to put these things together so that we may have a full-fledged economy, jobs, homes, food, clothing, and on top of that a social security programme adequately maintained and guaranteed because of a' proper basis in that kind of economy. That is the reason for the amendment moved by the leader of this group, which we are supporting, an amendment which points out that the government has failed to propose the fundamental social changes and economic planning which are necessary if we are to have full employment and if we are to provide and maintain adequate social security. -_ I should like to turn to something else that is along the line of social security. Apart from the fact that the speech from the throne makes only pious references to social security; apart from the fact that no basis has been provided for sustaining an adequate programme of social security, I should like to say to the government that if it wishes the country to think that it means business in the field of social security and) care of our people in time of need, there are certain, steps that the government can take without any further delay. I mention first of all old age pensions. It has already been demonstrated that the government can take action to make changes with respect to old age pensions, even changes with respect to the amount that is paid, by order in council, without seeking amendments to the old age pensions legislation. It has done so by raising the maximum amount payable

The Address-Mr. Knowles
to $25 a month. I urge again that members of the government realize that it is ridiculous, if not criminal, to ask our old people in this day and age, under living conditions as they are to-day, to try to exist on $25 a month. If I were to suggest that the Prime Minister, who will reach the age of seventy this year, should try it, I would be told that that is a ridiculous suggestion. I would be reminded that the Prime Minister has made a tremendous contribution to the well-being of Canada. Granted, but that is exactly the point we. are making. When our old people from coast to coast have reached the age of seventy they, too, have made a contribution to the welfare and to the well-being of this country, a contribution on the basis of which they deserve something better than $25 a month. Not only should the amount be raised to $30 or $40 a month, but the age limit most certainly ought to be lowered. If the government wants to argue that it should not do some of these things without bringing the matter before parliament, my first reply is, bring it before parliament and1 it will receive support without any question, I am sure, from all sides of this house.
But apart from that there are certain other things that the government could do without delay. Let me give a few details. According to the old age pensions legislation as it now stands a pensioner qualifies for his pension either on the day that he becomes seventy years of age or on the day that the old age pension authority in the province has received all of the necessary documents, whichever of those dates is the later. This means that in many a case an old age pensioner who was entitled to draw his pension from the day he was seventy years of age, must wait two or three months because of that technicality. I happen to know that some of the provincial governments have appealed to this government to change that regulation. I suggest that this should be done without delay.
Another point is that the act and the regulations as they now stand say that if a person becomes seventy-let us assume in this case the other qualification about getting all the papers in is in order-on the 1st day of March, he will draw his pension as from, the 1st day of March; but if seventy years ago the stork was two or three minutes late, so that a person becomes seventy on the 2nd day of March he does not draw his pension until as from the 1st day of April. There is no proportioning of the amount at all. I know that many a pensioner becomes utterly disillusioned! when he comes up against this fact, that he loses twenty-seven, twenty-eight or twenty-nine days of his pension, merely because he was not bom on the first day of the month.
There is another thing that bothers these people-and I stress these things, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me that this is the point of contact of many people with the government, and it is on the basis of this contact that people form their opinions about political democracy and government. I think it is highly important that we refrain from disillusioning and discouraging people in this way. Here is the case of a man who turned seventy in the month of December and became eligible for his pension as from January 1 of this year. Last year, when he was not on pension, despite his years and ill health he picked up $80 by doing odd jobs. This year there is no chance of his earning any money whatever, because of the condition of his health, but because he earned $80 last year the old age pension authority has to rule that he may earn $80 this year, which is $15 more than he is allowed to earn in addition to his pension in the province of Manitoba, so that the $15 or $1.25 a month is subtracted from his pension. Actually this man is not making any money this year, and will not make any; but when the year is over he will have no chance as long as he lives to pick up that meagre $15 that was deducted from his pension.
I might go on with other cases. I stress the point that this sort of thing is disillusioning to many people, and it is on this basis that many people form their opinion of democracy. It is high time that changes were made in the regulations respecting old age pensions.
Other matters that should be dealt with are the regulations concerning the transfer of property, liens on property, and all that sort of thing, which have made old age pensions only pre-death loans. I shall take only a sentence to refer to the blind, the deaf and other handicapped people. I support most heartily the appeal which has been made in this house on several occasions by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) that Canada do something more for these people.
I wish to say a word also on behalf of the veterans of the last war and their widows. I agree with the appeals that have been made during this debate on behalf of those being discharged from the services at the present time and those who will have to be demobilized when the war is over, but at the same time we must not forget the veterans of the last war and their widows. To my way of thinking the pension legislation, as well as the War Veterans' Allowance Act, needs to be overhauled. I know the story that is told of how generous this legislation is in many cases; but those I run up against appear to have attached to them strings of one kind or another by reason of which the veteran who has
The Address-Mr. Knowles

offered his life for his country finds that, though his later days are ruined as far as health is concerned, he can get nothing but a cold refusal on the ground of some technicality. Therefore I appeal for an overhauling of the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Similarly I want to make a further appeal on behalf of the widows of veterans of the last war. These do not form a very large group; politically they are not of special consequence in any particular constituency, but they deserve better treatment than we are giving them. The other day we welcomed the announcement by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) of a possible increase in the amount paid to these women. I call attention to the fact, however, that as yet this increase to $30 and a few cents a month has not been made basic for all these widows; the order in Council merely says that they may be paid up to that amount. I hope that order in council will be amended shortly by another that will make this amount, if not more, the basic payment to these widows. When this matter was before the house last year the minister promised or at least told us that while at that time we were only voting an item of money, this year he hoped to bring down legislation to care for these people on a permanent basis. I had hoped there might be some reference to such legislation in the speech from the throne, or by the minister if he took part in this debate, but as yet there has been no reference to it. Another point in connection with widows of veterans of the last war is that when the amount payable to them was increased the other day the ceiling on the total income they might have was not increased, except in the case of those who might have up to $25 a year of unearned income. The widow who in the past may have supplemented her allowance with a little money that she earned by going out and doing odd jobs may do so no longer, because the new regulation provides that she may receive up to $365 a year from the war veterans' allowance board provided she has no other income. In other words, the ceiling, apart from unearned income, is exactly where it was before this increase was made. I appeal as strongly as I can to the Minister of Pensions and National Health and to the government to take these matters under serious advisement.	. .
While on the subject of the widows I would stress also the difficulties we have been running into in connection with the provision that nothing can be given to the widow of a veteran unless that veteran saw service in an actual theatre of war. Does the minister not know that there are scores if not hundreds

of widows whose husbands got to England in the last war, some of whom were injured while on active service in England, but to whom nothing is available because of the definitions contained in the order in council? I appeal for the withdrawing of that line of distinction, which is working out as an unjust discrimination against a large number of these women.	[DOT]
I should like to turn for a moment or two now, Mr. Speaker, to the new wartime wages control order, order in council P.C. 9384. There is no reference to this order in council in the speech from the throne except the oblique reference to the necessity of maintaining wage stabilization. On the second day of this session, when I asked the Prime Minister if he would set aside a period for discussion of this order, he expressed doubt as to my inference that there was wide and active protest against it. I am sure he now knows that there is wide and active protest, for it has been expressed frequently on the floor of this house and the matter has been drawn to his attention in statements by members supporting the government not only in the house but even more bluntly outside the house, within the past few days. The reasons for labour's opposition to this order are well known. First of all there is the failure on the part of the government to consult labour before this order in council was brought down. There is also the fact that labour's representation on the national war labour board has been reduced from one in three to one in six Then there is the fact that the order makes possible the freezing of gross injustices, practically in so many words; for it is provided that nothing can be done about changing wage rates unless there are gross injustices or inequalities, and even then nothing can be done by way of raising those rates if that would increase the price of the product the manufacturer has to sell. The order also gives power to the national war labour board to reduce wages, to order a change from a time rate to a piece rate or, in that very lovely phrase of the order, an incentive rate. Then there are the provisions which are so drastic against labour's last resort, the strike weapon, and the other provisions which run so counter to British justice and which already have been brought to the attention of this house. I refer to the clauses which place the onus of proof of innocence upon the accused employee.
There is just one good thing about this order. It has united labour; it has shown labour the utter inability of a capitalist government to treat labour as a partner even in time of war. One hears rumours of

The Address-Mr. Knowles
various kinds around the halls of these buildings. I have been interested in the rumours that are circulating to the effect that the government may yet rescind this order and replace it with one not quite so drastic. Whether there is anything to these rumours or not, I do not know; but I certainly hope the government will do something in response to the appeals and protests, and that they will do it early, certainly before February 15 which, according to the terms of the order, is the date upon which it comes into full effect.
I should like now to turn to another matter bo which reference was not made in the speech from the throne, but which was introduced into the debate by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). I refer to the question of post-war civil aviation. The other day the hon. member roundly condemned the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) for refusing a licence to certain private interests which wanted to operate a service between Halifax and Saint John. I take the opposite view from the hon. member for York-Sunbury, and in this instance I am going to commend the Minister of Munitions and Supply for his action. I say quite frankly that my reason for offering my commendation is that I learned from an editorial in the Montreal Gazette that the private enterprise which sought the licence was none other than the Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
But while I commend the minister for his action in that instance, I am afraid I have no option but to follow my commendation with condemnation of the government for its action, particularly in the north and1 northwest, by means of which it is literally giving away to this privately-owned concern, Canadian Pacific Air Lines, something that is of great value to us-our northern country. Speaking in terms of aviation, the value of our great north country is obvious, as far as international flying is concerned. I should like, too, to stress the fact that there is also in that area great value domestically. There is a tremendous amount of mineral wealth in that great north, country, and possibilities for settlement beyond our dreams. Yet at the present time, the air being practically the only means of communication with that country, we are literally giving it over to this privately-owned enterprise which, incidentally, has a very interesting tie-up with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, in the matter of aviation there is no such thing as private enterprise. Private enterprise in flying would mean that every individual concern would
build its own airports, would establish its own meteorological services, would set up its own radio beams. What a hodge-podge we would have 1 Under such a set-up where would there be safety for the travelling public in this new means of transport?
Hon. members know what has been done. The people of Canada through their government, and rightly so, have invested huge sums of money-I believe our investment is now at least $200,000,000, if not more-in the building of airports, lighting facilities, radio, meteorological services and the like. Actually, flying is a public service which the public, through government funds, has to make possible. I call as my witness for this view none other than one of the former leaders of the Conservative party in this house, the Right Hon. R. B., now Viscount, Bennett. Hon. members who were in the house in those days or who have studied the debates for 1937 will recall that when the Trans-Canada Air Lines bill was before the house the then Right Hon. Mr. Beqpett appealed to the government not to give away something then held by the people of this country. As a matter of fact it appears that he was able to exert some influence upon the government at that time. I call not only Viscount Bennett as witness, but also the Winnipeg Free Press, which has been quite definite on this point. Although I have not time to quote from it, I have before me an article which appeared in that newspaper on May 12, 1943, entitled "TCA versus CPA". The Free Press points out that so far as flying on main line and international lines is concerned, there is simply no such thing as private enterprise. The people have a basic interest and concern in this matter, which must not be given away.
We should realize that aviation can add tremendously to the wealth of Canada. It is not just a matter of having planes available for the use of a few individuals who need to make a quick trip. Planes, like trains, can add to the wealth of our country and the people in it, even though many of those people may never travel by plane. We must see to it that the wealth which can be added to the life of this country by this new means of transportation and communication is not given away to private enterprise, and I appeal to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, whom I have already commended for his action in one respect, to take this matter under serious advisement, lest we find that we have given away something which should be held for the people of Canada.
If I may add just one further word in this connection, I would mention the international
The Address-Mr. Knowles

field, concerning which I feel the government of the day should take certain steps. This is a matter of great importance to Canada. Frankly, if private monopolies in various countries are able to put over the idea of what is miscalled freedom of the air, so that private companies are free to fly anywhere and everywhere, Canada stands to lose. If we go to the other extreme and build a fence around each country, so that the national lines of various countries can fly only within their own borders, again Canada stands to lose. There is one basis upon which Canada stands to gain. The one basis upon which our geographical position, valuable as it is, will not be circumvented, is in international control of the international air routes of the world.
In that connection I wish to refer to an announcement made by the Australian High Commisisoner to Canada on January 24, in which he drew the attention of this country to an agreement signed on January 21 of this year by representatives of the governments of New Zealand and Australia. Let me quote one or two of the more important paragraphs of this New Zeal and-Australian agreement:
(17)	The two governments agree that the regulation of all air transport services should be subject to the terms of a convention which will supersede the convention relating to the regulation of aerial navigation.
(18)	The two governments declare that the air services using the international air trunk routes should be operated by an international air transport authority.
There are in the agreement other sections of equal importance. I have not time to read them, but I am earnestly hoping that at an early date the government will take a stand similar to that which these two governments have taken, lest Canada find herself, despite our present favoured geographical position, out in the cold.
In closing. I understand the vote may be taken to-night or to-morrow. Our subamendment, coming first, will naturally have the support of this group, to a man, because we believe that it expresses what is basically missing from the speech from the throne. We believe it expresses the view of the people of Canada that the time has come for fundamental social and economic change.
If, perchance, our amendment is defeated, we come then to the Progressive Conservative amendment. We are not satisfied with it; that is why the leader of this group moved a subamendment. However, it states some things which are very obvious. Boiled down, the substance of the Progressive Conservative

amendment states that the government has failed. Well, that is fairly obvious, so that we shall support that amendment as well.
If, perchance, that amendment is likewise defeated, and we are left with the address itself, then we have no option but to accept it, not because we are satisfied with the speech from the throne, by any means, but because we feel that at this stage of the game, surely anything less would be unthinkable. If the proposals which the government has made in the speech from the throne are endorsed by a vote in this house to-night or to-morrow, and if it does not want them to backfire, I suggest that the government not merely be content with pious promises but consider seriously reducing these proposals into legislation to be enacted before this session ends.
I suggest also that the government without any delay rescind the obnoxious order in council, P.C. 9384, and! replace it with a democratic labour policy.
I suggest also that the government do something without further delay on behalf of the groups I have mentioned, the aged, the blind pensioners, the widows of veterans of the last war, the veterans themselves of the last war, those who are being discharged from the services now, and others who would be covered by a social security programme. Even then it would only be scratching the surface. Even then a great deal would be left for succeeding governments to do, and we shall leave it to the people to say what government shall succeed the present one. But if we are to win not only the war but the peace, surely the present government should do nothing less than to meet the requests that we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have set forth in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne rightly emphasizes the fact that the winning of the war remains the first objective of the Canadian people. No government and no Canadian can hold any other view so long as we are engaged in this struggle; for despite the fact that we are now in the fifth year of the war no one seems to be any too certain that the war's end is anywhere in sight. For that reason I heartily concur in the statement made in the speech from the throne concerning the prosecution of the war.
Post-war reconstruction can be divided into three distinct phases. The immediate phase will be the gradual demobilization of the armed forces; the intermediate phase will be the period of reconstruction and rehabilitation, and the third phase will be the long-range planning of our economic development.

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
Before dealing with these three phases I assert, after listening to the numerous speeches which have been delivered in this house during the last few days, that neither will a reactionary philosophy satisfy the needs of the Canadian people in the post-war period nor will the philosophy of the extreme left satisfy those needs. No one would argue that the people of Canada would stand for the reactionary philosophy of pre-war days or that it would be fair and just to our people. On the other hand, no one will tell us that everything that has been built up over centuries of progress must be thrown overboard and something else substituted in its stead, although, of course, the advocates of that philosophy seem to be certain that it would work like a charm..
Social credit?
Social credit is one philosophy that can solve the problems of this nation, yes.
And it is not as vicious as some philosophies.

I repeat, reaction will not satisfy the needs of the Canadian people in the post-war world, nor will the other extreme do it. But we of the Social Credjt group believe that there are many good things which must be preserved, things which have been handed down to us over the ages. On the other hand, we believe that some change is absolutely necessary. We believe that reform is essential. We believe that our proposals with respect to the supply of purchasing power for our people will solve the problems before us.
But, as I said, the immediate post-war problem will be that of demobilization and the transition from war-time to peace-time production. Undoubtedly this will be a period of confusion. Our industries will have to be readjusted and our factory workers and war-time civil servants will have to be assisted in finding profitable occupations. Our returned soldiers must be reestablished in our national life and be guaranteed allowances as well as gratuities. What is more, they must be guaranteed security.
Canadian agriculture must be placed upon such a basis as to guarantee to the farmer a fair standard of living. It must be remembered that one-third of our total population is engaged in agriculture.
Our aged people must also be provided for. No longer must the Canadian people tolerate the conditions which existed in the past and which still exist with respect to our old age pensions. Reference has been made by a number of hon. members to the fact that the amount of the old age pension is inadequate.
A great number of people with whom I come in contact and who have asked my assistance in this matter are in their late sixties, and some of them are in such a state of health that they cannot possibly make their own living. Yet these Canadian pioneers, as the law stands today, are not entitled to receive the old age pension just because they do not happen to be seventy years of age. I feel that that is an extreme injustice to our pioneers. I consider that anyone at the age of sixty or over who is physically incapable of making a living should be granted an old age pension.
Then let me mention our youth. On numerous occasions I have read statements in the newspapers that young people between the ages ' of eighteen and twenty-one should not be granted the right to vote because they are immature, their judgments are immature, and it is best in a democracy to let them grow up to the age of twenty-one before they are given an opportunity to vote. But I would point out that it is these young men who were called upon first to serve this country in time of war. I know that some individuals in certain quarters are afraid that these, young men will be too impulsive, that they may not accept the same old promises in the same spirit as those who carry heavier responsibilities, or something of the like. But I maintain that after this war our young people of the age of eighteen and over should be allowed to vote.
Mention has been made of the condition of the blind and other individuals who through physical incapacity cannot look after themselves. If we are a civilized nation we should so amend the existing legislation as to provide pensions for these unfortunate people, regardless of their age. This is something which we should do immediately.
In my opinion the period of post-war reconstruction will find us unprepared. I believe that the promises which are being made almost daily, and so liberally, will amount to very little and will bring results which will greatly disappoint our people.
I do not intend to deal to-night with the subject of rehabilitation of our fighting men; I hope to have an opportunity to discuss that particular subject on another occasion. But I wish to say something with regard to agriculture.
We have come to a point where every political group in Canada should state its policy clearly to the people. No longer must political parties aim at catching votes in confusion. Every group should take its stand on all important problems, giving the people
The Address-Mr. Hlynka

the opportunity democratically to choose that philosophy which they believe will give them the results they desire.
I have touched so far on the first phase of post-war reconstruction. The second phase is the intermediate period of reconstruction and rehabilitation. I know that in the speech from the throne industry is promised considerable assistance. Personally I have nothing against that; I believe that it is a proper stand to take. This is what the speech says:
Suitable peace-time uses for war plants are being sought, and plans are being made for their speedy conversion. To assist in the conversion of war plants and in the development of small and medium-scale industrial enterprises, the provision of additional credit facilities, for both fixed and working capital, will be required. To meet this need, your approval will be sought for the establishment of an industrial development bank as a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada. Expenditures on developmental work, in preparation for the transition of industry from war to peace, will be encouraged by suitable tax modifications.
Now let me read the promise which is given to our farmers. This is all I can find in the entire length of the throne speech:
To ensure economic stability for agriculture, you will be asked to make provision for a price floor for staple farm products.
Nothing else is said about agriculture. Let me emphasize that I have no doubt that the present government will assist industry when it comes to the period of adjustment, the period when concerns will have to change and tune-up for peace-time production. With this policy I agree. But why not give the same consideration to our farmers? Why should the farmers be penalized to the extent that they are actually ignored? The only thing that is promised to them is a floor under agricultural prices-a floor! What that floor will be, no one knows; it may be fair, it may be poor. No mention is made of other problems which face agriculture. Let us see to it that the government offers the farmer something which will make farming a profitable occupation.
If one were to analyse the attitude throughout the years of our federal governments toward agriculture, it would be found that they have failed agriculture in every respect. In my opinion at least five things should be guaranteed to agriculture. I mentioned that one-third of our total population is engaged in this calling; surely they deserve a more sympathetic consideration than is being given them by the government.
The forecast which is made in- the speech from the throne is only a straw in the wind. The farmer should be guaranteed parity prices

which will ensure to him the income he needs to buy the things that are necessary for the maintenance of a decent standard of living. Unless agriculture receives an adequate income, no one can possibly expect the farmer to be able to pay his debts, to educate his children, to carry on efficiently and, in addition to that, to put by the odd cent for a rainy day. Under those conditions that is an utter impossibility. The farmer must have an adequate share of the national income.
In the second place, a definite long-range policy in Tigard to grain and live stock production should be introduced. As it is to-day -and many hon. members have referred to it-the farmer gets by day in and day out, but he does not know what order he may expect from the government.
In the third place, a comprehensive scheme of non-contributory crop insurance is necessary. I say that many farmers in the west have suffered greatly because of the odd bad year, because of frost, hail and other hazards of nature, and it takes the farmer years to get back on his feet again. Surely the government is in a position to give the farmers a non-contributory insurance.
