Thank you, Mr. Speaker. We
hear on the one hand that after the war Canada should continue to share in this imperial federation which we have been in for so long a time, and on the other hand we are told, as an encouragement to support the struggle, that after the war there will be a . sort of international body composed of the allied nations, and in which the small nations will be on an equal footing with the larger ones. That would be a very fine thing for Canada as a peace policy and in so far as her international trade and commerce are concerned. That is all very well; but when one considers the opportunities that the government has had up to now to prove its sincerity, and has not taken advantage of any of them, how can we now believe in such statements? Why should a certain class of people start moves to bring Canada within an imperial federation to which most of the Canadian people are opposed?
Since the beginning of the war we have had quite a few interallied conferences. We were told that Canada entered this war as an independent nation under the signature of her own king, and that we were fighting the axis as such. After the war began there was concerted action to impose the conscription of men for overseas service. There was an effort made to get everything possible from Canada in the way of blood, money, or other sacrifices. Let us see now what was going on in the meantime. There was a conference which took place on the Atlantic ocean. At that conference there was drawn up what was called the Atlantic charter which is supposed to be the basis of governing all the democratic countries when the war is over. Was Canada asked to take part in that conference as an independent country? Was the Canadian Prime Minister

The Address-Mr. Roy
invited to that conference? No. As I say, we were told that it was a charter for all the allied countries after the war is over. We had another conference at Washington and yet Canada was not there. We had a conference at Casablanca and we find that it was just like the others. There was no place there for Canada. No attention was paid to Canada at all. We were just a negligible quantity. Since then we have had another conference at Teheran. At this conference China, Russia, the United States and Great Britain were represented. Canada, being the fourth largest power in the war, was not represented by its Prime Minister.	There was no place for
Canada at all, although she is in the war with all her resources. What had then become of our independence? And who was speaking for Canada at those conferences? The British Prime Minister? Before the Teheran conference was called we had a conference which was advertised in the newspapers as a tripartite conference.* It was held in Quebec city. We were very well satisfied with the choice of Quebec city as the site of that conference. We were pleased to receive such distinguished visitors. As I say, this was advertised as a tripartite conference, but, although it was held in Quebec city and although our Prime Minister was there, the resulting decisions of that conference were signed only by the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States. Canada was again excluded. Although Canada was excluded, did we hear any protests, or criticism such as we heard for the establishment of conscription and for an all-out war effort? We have not heard any complaint at all from anyone. It is amazing. We have not enough pride to demand our place at these conferences.
The next paragraph will read as follows:
Failed to undertake public works to prevent the already existing unemployment.
I should like to comment on this subject to a certain extent. According to the figures which were published recently in some official publication of the government, and according to a statement which was made not very long ago by the deputy controller of the national selective service commission, we shall have before the month of June some 100,000 workers dismissed from the war industrial plants; therefore, unemployment will prevail again. We have a proof of that in Quebec city, where, according to what I have been told by responsible authorities, nearly 2,000 men are unemployed to-day and there will be about 6,000 or 7,000 unemployed in two months' time. This supports well my point that unemployment has already reappeared in Canada.
For two years we have been told an awful lot about reconstruction works, about post-war plans to give work to everybody in Canada; we have been told that unemployment would not come back, that the government was to prevent the return to a state of things such as existed in the depression years we lived through before the war. As I said a while ago, the government has had many opportunities to show its sincerity but we are already facing unemployment. I say that the government should have undertaken public works to prevent unemployment and to serve other purposes.
This brings me to a project which was investigated last summer by a French writer whose name is well-known throughout Canada, Mr. Robert Rumilly. Mr. Rumilly was asked by some concern to undertake a complete investigation and to inquire as to all the possibilities that could be offered by Gaspe peninsula in view of the post-war reconstruction, and the report of his investigation was published by Le Soleil, a newspaper of Quebec, supporting the government and by La Nouvelliste, a newspaper of Three Rivers, also supporting the government. All his findings were published, and to make a long story short his report suggested the construction of a railroad running through the interior of the Gaspe peninsula, in order to shorten the distance to Gaspe harbour, which should be properly organized as a winter seaport. If these works were undertaken to-day, in the first place they would take care of the unemployment situation perhaps for the whole province of Quebec. In the second place the construction of this railroad would; permit the development of the mineral deposits in the interior of Gaspesia, and I believe the exploitation of the resources of the Gaspe peninsula alone would be enough to justify the construction of this line. That is not all however. It would also offer a shorter road to the Atlantic than the one actually existing between Winnipeg and Halifax, and facilitate the export of our Canadian wheat to the European market.
I have some figures, Mr. Speaker, which I am sure will interest you and especially hon. members from western Canada. I have said that the construction of a railroad and the opening of Gaspe harbour as a winter seaport would solve the question of the export of wheat which has not found its solution yet. Let me prove that statement. The distance from Winnipeg to Halifax is approximately 2,200 miles, while the distance from Winnipeg to Gaspe, if this railroad were built, would be about 1,930 miles. According to the Canadian National Railways the freight rate on wheat

from Winnipeg to Halifax is forty-three cents per hundred pounds, or within a small fraction of twenty-six cents a bushel. If you take off 270 miles from the distance between Winnipeg and Halifax, this would amount to one-eighth of the total distance, and if you carry* that int.o the cost per bushel it would mean a saving of almost exactly three cents. If our total exports of wheat after the war should amount to about 300,000,000 bushels annually, and if half that quantity should be shipped by way of Gaspe, it would mean a saving of some $4,500,000 annually for the western farmers; this would represent interest on a capital investment of $150,000,000, or much more than would be required for the construction of that railroad, which would be 160 miles in length, and the work at the seaport.
I have given the distance and rates from Winnipeg to Halifax over the Canadian National Railways. Perhaps hon. members would be interested in knowing the freight rates on other routes we sometimes use for the shipment of wheat. The rate from Winnipeg to New York via the Canadian National Railways is fifty-three cents per hundred pounds, as compared with forty-three cents to Halifax and thirty-eight cents to Gaspe. The rate from Winnipeg to Albany is fifty-two cents, via the Canadian National, while the rate via the Canadian Pacific from Winnipeg to New York is 50i cents per hundred pounds and to Albany fifty-three cents. So that it is more* expensive to ship wheat via New York and Albany in the winter than by Halifax. Then I might give the distance between New York, Halifax, Gaspe and Liverpool. The distance from Halifax to Liverpool is 2,475 miles, and from New York to Liverpool, 3,119 miles, while from Gaspe to Liverpool it is 2,450 miles via St. John's, Newfoundland, and 2,300 miles via the strait of Belle Isle. These figures would show that Gaspe offers Canada a great opportunity to solve the difficulties of export, and to help the solution of our railroad problem in peace time; they confirm the wisdom of the advice which was given for more than one hundred years by engineers and even by the British admiralty, that the Gaspe seaport is the commercial and military key of Canada. If we would recognize this truth we would be able to organize our transportation system in such a way that the wheat of the west would compete in the international market. Of course the advantages I have mentioned would apply not only to wheat, or to outward traffic, but to all our traffic, inward as well as outward.
The last paragraph of the amendment I intend to move reads as follows:
Failed to grant farmers and fishermen exemption from military service, in order to remove from them the vexatious proceedings resulting? from the narrow application of the national selective service regulations.
The hon. member who preceded me rightly said that everyone would know where he stood after having heard what he had to say. I think my stand on this question is also well known. In 1942 I moved amendments asking for the exemption of farmers, but I received very little support. At the following session there were loud cries heard from all corners of the house about the shortage of manpower for the cutting of fuel wood and also on our farms. I have in my hand sessional paper 135. This contains only a few of the letters sent to the Department of Labour and the Department of Agriculture by municipal councils, county councils and agricultural organizations in Ontario and the western provinces. When the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) asked for the production of these documents he was requested to go to the department and choose what he wmnted, because there were cabinets containing thousands of these requests from all over Canada, and they were too numerous to be all produced. So we have here requests from Ontario and the western provinces, with only two from Quebec in this lot. These ask for the exemption of farmers, or for a regulation by national selective service with respect to the calling up of draftees, so that the man-power on farms might not be disturbed. Taking into account this general and huge protest, I believe I was quite right in asking for the exemption of farmers. In fact, I am now more convinced when, in the last few days, I have heard from different parts of the house hon. members reproaching the government for keeping more than 60,000 men under arms in Canada, when they are not needed. The government is being asked to dismiss these men. Well, if we do not need them, why do we keep them? Why does national selective service keep calling men every day, if we do not need them. Why do we call them if we have already too many, and if their being called is useless and a bad thing for the country?
In order that I may have time to move my amendment, I shall not speak at greater length this evening but shall complete on another occasion what I had intended to say. I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion):

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend this evening to discuss the merits of the amendment, but in my humble view it is out of order. I understand that in our parliamentary code there are no precise and definite rules respecting the form of such an amendment, but I have always felt that, to be legal, it cannot be worded as is this one. We find in it these words:
I have the honour to move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) that the following words be added to the amendment.
I draw particular attention to the words "that the following words be added to the amendment", and humbly submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member is out of order in asking that something be added to the amendment of the Tory- party. Had the amendment now before the Chair asked that something be stricken out, and that such part be replaced by something else, then we would have before us a proper amendment. But now we have before us only a completion of the amendment offered by the Tory party.
